laws.title: Islamic Republic Constitution — Velayat-e Faqih
laws.subtitle: Supreme Leader holds highest authority under Islamic jurisprudence
laws.fullDescription: Iran's 1979 Constitution, revised in 1989, establishes the Islamic Republic based on the principle of Velayat-e Faqih (Guardianship of the Islamic Jurist). The Supreme Leader (currently Ali Khamenei) holds supreme authority over all branches of government, the military, judiciary, and media. The President and parliament are elected but operate within constraints set by unelected bodies. The Guardian Council vets candidates for elections, rejecting those deemed insufficiently Islamic.
laws.penalty: N/A — constitutional structure
exceptions: Elected bodies have limited autonomy within the framework
Some civil society space exists within approved boundaries
laws.source: Constitution of the Islamic Republic of Iran, 1979 (revised 1989)

quiz.q: What principle grants the Supreme Leader of Iran ultimate authority?
options: Velayat-e Faqih (Guardianship of the Islamic Jurist)
quiz.explanation: Velayat-e Faqih (Guardianship of the Islamic Jurist) is the constitutional principle that places the Supreme Leader at the apex of Iran's political system, with authority over all branches of government, military, and judiciary.

laws.title: Qisas — Retributive Justice
laws.subtitle: Islamic law of equal retaliation for bodily harm
laws.fullDescription: Iran's Penal Code incorporates Qisas (retributive justice/eye for an eye), derived from Islamic law. Under Qisas provisions, victims or their families can demand equivalent punishment for bodily harm — if someone causes another to lose an eye, the victim can demand the perpetrator's eye be removed. For murder, the victim's family can demand execution (Qisas al-nafs) or accept blood money (Diya). Families can also grant pardons. This system has been criticized by international human rights organizations.
laws.penalty: Equivalent physical punishment or execution for intentional bodily harm/murder; alternatively blood money (Diya)
exceptions: Victim family can pardon and accept Diya (blood money) instead
Cases where perpetrator is a parent (parent cannot be executed for killing child in traditional interpretation)
laws.source: Iranian Islamic Penal Code, 2013, Book One

quiz.q: What alternative to Qisas punishment can victims accept under Iranian law?
quiz.explanation: Under Iranian law's Qisas provisions, victims or their families can choose to accept Diya (blood money) as compensation instead of demanding equivalent physical punishment or execution, giving families significant power in criminal outcomes.

laws.title: Hudud Offenses — Fixed Punishments
laws.subtitle: Mandatory Islamic criminal punishments
laws.fullDescription: Iran's Penal Code includes Hudud (fixed punishments mandated by Islamic law) for specific offenses: amputation for theft (under strict conditions rarely applied in practice), flogging for alcohol consumption (80 lashes), flogging for extramarital sexual relations (100 lashes for unmarried, stoning for married under specific conditions), and death for adultery under certain evidentiary standards. International human rights bodies have condemned these punishments as torture.
laws.penalty: Amputation, flogging (80-100 lashes), stoning, or death depending on offense
exceptions: Strict evidentiary requirements (4 witnesses for some offenses) make application difficult in practice
Judges have discretion to impose Ta'zir (discretionary) penalties instead in many cases
laws.source: Iranian Islamic Penal Code, 2013, Book Two (Hudud)

quiz.q: How many lashes does Iranian law prescribe for alcohol consumption under Hudud?
quiz.explanation: Under Iran's Islamic Penal Code, consumption of alcohol is a Hudud offense carrying 80 lashes. A third offense can carry the death penalty. In practice, not all convicted individuals receive the full punishment.

laws.title: Women's Rights — Legal Discrimination
laws.subtitle: Systematic gender discrimination in law
laws.fullDescription: Iranian law contains numerous provisions that discriminate against women: a woman's testimony in court is worth half that of a man in many cases; a daughter inherits half what a son inherits; blood money (Diya) for a woman's death is half that for a man; women must obtain a husband's permission to travel abroad and work; child custody after divorce defaults to fathers after age 7 (sons) and age 2 (daughters). The mandatory hijab law requires all women in public to wear the headscarf.
laws.penalty: Various criminal and civil disadvantages built into the legal system
exceptions: Women have full legal capacity to enter contracts
Women can be judges in some lower court positions (recent reform)
Female doctors and professionals operate with professional autonomy
laws.source: Iranian Civil Code; Islamic Penal Code

quiz.q: Under Iranian law, how does a woman's inheritance compare to a man's for the same relationship (e.g., daughter vs son)?
options: A woman inherits twice as much
A daughter inherits half what a son inherits
Inheritance depends on the woman's age
quiz.explanation: Under Iranian inheritance law, a daughter inherits half of what a son inherits from the same parent, reflecting traditional Islamic inheritance rules codified in Iranian law that have been criticized for gender discrimination.

laws.title: LGBTQ+ Criminalization
laws.subtitle: Death penalty possible for same-sex relations
laws.fullDescription: Same-sex sexual activity is criminalized in Iran and can carry the death penalty. Iranian law prescribes execution for homosexual intercourse (lavat) between men and flogging for lesser same-sex acts. Several executions of men for homosexual conduct have been documented since the 1979 revolution. Iran does permit gender reassignment surgery, in a unique approach that treats gender dysphoria as a medical condition while maintaining that homosexuality is a crime. LGBTQ+ Iranians face persecution and many have fled the country.
laws.penalty: Death penalty for homosexual intercourse; flogging for lesser same-sex acts
exceptions: Gender reassignment surgery is legal and state-funded
Those identifying as transgender may receive medical treatment
laws.source: Iranian Islamic Penal Code, 2013, Articles 233-240

quiz.q: What is Iran's unusual policy regarding transgender persons compared to its stance on homosexuality?
options: Transgender persons are executed while gay persons are only flogged
Gender reassignment surgery is legal and state-funded while homosexual acts remain criminalized
quiz.explanation: Iran has an unusual dual approach: same-sex sexual activity is criminalized (potentially carrying the death penalty), while gender reassignment surgery is legal and even state-funded, treating gender dysphoria as a medical condition.

laws.title: Mandatory Hijab Law
laws.subtitle: Compulsory Islamic dress code for women
laws.fullDescription: Iranian law requires all women (including foreigners) to wear the hijab (headscarf) in public. The Islamic Penal Code punishes women for 'bad hijab' (improper covering). Enforcement intensified after the 2022 Mahsa Amini protests, when 22-year-old Mahsa Amini died in morality police custody after being arrested for improper hijab. The resulting protests (Woman, Life, Freedom movement) were the largest in Iran since the 1979 revolution, resulting in the deaths of hundreds of protesters.
laws.penalty: Fines and imprisonment up to 10 years for repeated violations (under strengthened 2023 law)
exceptions: Non-Muslim foreigners face same requirements
Women at home and in private spaces exempt
Requirements apply in all public spaces including cars
laws.source: Iranian Islamic Penal Code; Hijab Law (2023 amendments)

quiz.q: What event in 2022 sparked Iran's largest protests since 1979?
options: Mahsa Amini's death in morality police custody for improper hijab
quiz.explanation: The death of 22-year-old Mahsa Amini in morality police custody in 2022, after being arrested for 'improper hijab,' sparked the 'Woman, Life, Freedom' protests — the largest in Iran since the 1979 revolution.

laws.title: Press and Media Law — Censorship
laws.subtitle: Extensive state control of media and internet
laws.fullDescription: Iran's Press Law and Cybercrime Law impose extensive restrictions on media freedom. Iran consistently ranks near the bottom of global press freedom indices. The state controls broadcast media entirely. Newspapers and websites require licenses and can be shut down by courts at the government's request. Social media platforms (Instagram, Telegram, WhatsApp, YouTube) are blocked or filtered. Iran has developed a national intranet ('National Information Network') as an alternative to the open internet. Many journalists are imprisoned.
laws.penalty: Imprisonment up to 10 years for press offenses; death penalty in extreme cases of 'spreading corruption on earth'
exceptions: State media and approved media operate freely
VPN use to circumvent filtering is widespread but technically illegal
laws.source: Iranian Press Law; Cybercrime Law 2009

quiz.q: What has Iran developed as an alternative to the open internet?
quiz.explanation: Iran has developed a 'National Information Network' (sometimes called the 'halal internet' by critics) as a domestic intranet alternative to the open internet, aiming to reduce dependence on foreign internet infrastructure.

laws.title: Moharebeh — Enmity Against God
laws.subtitle: Capital offense for opposition to the state
laws.fullDescription: Moharebeh (enmity against God/waging war against God) is a capital offense in Iran's Islamic Penal Code. The charge has been applied broadly to political dissidents, protesters, and members of opposition groups. It was used extensively against protesters from the 2022 Woman, Life, Freedom movement, with several protesters executed for moharebeh. The charge of 'spreading corruption on earth' (Ifsad fel-arz) is similarly broad and capital. International human rights organizations have condemned these charges as tools for political suppression.
laws.penalty: Death penalty
exceptions: Repentance before arrest may be accepted as a defense in theory
Diplomatic pressure has led to some reprieves
laws.source: Iranian Islamic Penal Code, 2013, Articles 279-287

quiz.q: For what purpose has Iran's charge of Moharebeh (enmity against God) been broadly applied?
options: To prosecute political dissidents and protesters
quiz.explanation: Iran's charge of Moharebeh has been broadly applied to political dissidents, protesters from movements including the 2022 Woman, Life, Freedom protests, and members of opposition groups, resulting in executions of protesters.

laws.title: Personal Status Law — Marriage Under Islamic Law
laws.subtitle: Marriage governed by Islamic personal law
laws.fullDescription: Iran's Civil Code governs personal status under Islamic law. The minimum age for marriage is 13 for girls and 15 for boys (with judicial permission for younger). Men can take up to four wives simultaneously (polygamy). A husband can divorce his wife unilaterally through talaq. Women must go through court to divorce and face much higher hurdles. Women's right to divorce is restricted to specific grounds including the husband's impotence, absence, or failure to provide. Mut'a (temporary marriage) is also recognized.
laws.penalty: Criminal penalties for marriage below minimum age without judicial permission
exceptions: Court permission required for marriages below the standard minimum age
Mut'a (temporary marriage) recognized as a separate institution
laws.source: Iranian Civil Code, Articles 1034-1256

quiz.q: What is the minimum age for marriage of girls under Iranian law?
quiz.explanation: Iran's Civil Code sets the minimum marriage age at 13 for girls and 15 for boys, with judicial permission allowing marriage at even younger ages, drawing widespread international criticism for enabling child marriage.

laws.title: Internet Censorship and VPN Laws
laws.subtitle: Filtering of internet and criminalization of circumvention
laws.fullDescription: Iran maintains one of the world's most extensive internet censorship systems, filtering social media, news sites, and content deemed un-Islamic or politically sensitive. Instagram, Facebook, Twitter/X, YouTube, and WhatsApp are blocked (though widely accessed via VPNs). The use of VPNs is technically illegal but enforcement is selective. The Cybercrime Law criminalizes accessing banned content. Following the 2022 protests, internet shutdowns were used as a tool of repression. Iran has increased bandwidth of the national intranet.
laws.penalty: Fines and imprisonment for producing or distributing banned content; lesser penalties for personal VPN use
exceptions: Government employees may legally access filtered content for official purposes
Certain businesses may receive filtered-site exemptions
laws.source: Iranian Cybercrime Law, 2009; Internet Filtering Regulations

quiz.q: What is the legal status of VPN use to circumvent internet filtering in Iran?
quiz.explanation: VPN use to circumvent internet filtering is technically illegal under Iran's Cybercrime Law, but enforcement is selective — millions of Iranians use VPNs daily to access blocked social media despite the legal prohibition.

laws.title: Nuclear Program — Sanctions Law
laws.subtitle: International sanctions regime affecting daily life
laws.fullDescription: Iran's nuclear program has resulted in extensive international sanctions imposed by the US, EU, and UN Security Council. While not domestic law per se, these sanctions severely affect Iran's economy and daily life. Iranian oil exports are severely restricted, the Iranian rial has lost significant value, and access to international banking is cut off. Iran's own domestic law requires continued nuclear development as a national right. The 2015 JCPOA (nuclear deal) temporarily relieved some sanctions before the US withdrew in 2018.
laws.penalty: International sanctions affect the entire economy; domestic law criminalizes compliance with certain US sanctions
exceptions: Humanitarian goods (medicine, food) theoretically exempt from sanctions
JCPOA participation temporarily waived some sanctions
laws.source: UN Security Council Resolutions; JCPOA 2015; US IEEPA and CISADA sanctions

quiz.q: What happened to the 2015 JCPOA nuclear deal?
options: It is still fully in force
The US withdrew from it in 2018
It was replaced by a stronger deal in 2020
quiz.explanation: The US withdrew from the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action (JCPOA) in 2018 under President Trump, reimposing sanctions that had been relieved under the deal, leading to Iran gradually reducing its compliance with the agreement's nuclear restrictions.

laws.title: Religious Minorities — Legal Status
laws.subtitle: Non-Muslims face legal discrimination
laws.fullDescription: Iran's constitution recognizes Zoroastrians, Jews, and Christians as protected religious minorities. However, non-Muslims face legal discrimination: blood money (Diya) for a non-Muslim's death is lower than for a Muslim; apostasy (leaving Islam) can carry the death penalty; proselytizing to Muslims is illegal; non-Muslims cannot marry Muslims; and certain government positions are restricted to Muslims. Bahá'ís are not recognized as a minority and face severe persecution.
laws.penalty: Death penalty for male apostasy; imprisonment for female apostasy; death or imprisonment for proselytizing
exceptions: Recognized minorities (Christian, Jewish, Zoroastrian) can practice their religion privately
Protected minorities have reserved parliamentary seats
laws.source: Iranian Constitution, Article 13; Islamic Penal Code

quiz.q: Which religious group in Iran is NOT recognized as a protected minority and faces severe persecution?
quiz.explanation: While Iran's constitution recognizes Jews, Christians, and Zoroastrians as protected religious minorities with reserved parliamentary seats, Bahá'ís are not recognized and face severe persecution including property confiscation, imprisonment, and denial of higher education.

laws.title: Death Penalty — Execution Rate
laws.subtitle: One of the world's highest execution rates
laws.fullDescription: Iran has one of the world's highest execution rates. In 2022 and 2023, Iran executed over 500 people per year — more than any other country except China in raw numbers. Executions are carried out for drug trafficking, murder, rape, armed robbery, and political offenses. The execution of juvenile offenders (those who were minors at the time of the offense) continues despite international law prohibitions. Public hangings have been used for deterrence.
laws.penalty: Death by hanging (most common), firing squad, or stoning
exceptions: Juvenile offenders technically protected (2013 Penal Code reforms) but exceptions widely used
Insanity defense available
Pardon from Supreme Leader possible in exceptional cases
laws.source: Iranian Islamic Penal Code; Amnesty International Annual Reports

quiz.q: Approximately how many people did Iran execute annually in 2022-2023?
quiz.explanation: Iran executed over 500 people per year in both 2022 and 2023, making it one of the world's leading executioners by absolute number, surpassed only by China. Executions include drug offenses, murder, and political crimes.

laws.title: Judicial System — Revolutionary Courts
laws.subtitle: Parallel court system for political and security cases
laws.fullDescription: Iran has a parallel court system including Revolutionary Courts that handle national security, political, and drug cases. Revolutionary Courts operate with reduced procedural protections compared to regular courts. The Supreme Court and Court of Appeal provide appellate review. The Head of the Judiciary is appointed by the Supreme Leader. Iran's judiciary has been used extensively to suppress political opposition, with thousands of dissidents, journalists, and activists prosecuted. The 2022 protest trials were conducted rapidly with minimal defense access.
laws.penalty: Revolutionary Court sentences range from flogging to death penalty
exceptions: Regular criminal courts handle non-political matters with more standard procedures
International pressure occasionally leads to reduced sentences
laws.source: Iranian Constitution, Articles 156-174; Law on Organization of Courts

quiz.q: Who appoints the Head of Iran's Judiciary?
quiz.explanation: The Head of Iran's Judiciary is appointed by the Supreme Leader for 5-year terms, ensuring that the judicial system remains aligned with the Supreme Leader's authority and the principles of Velayat-e Faqih.

laws.title: Apostasy — Leaving Islam
laws.subtitle: Death penalty for abandoning Islam
laws.fullDescription: Apostasy (ridda — leaving Islam) is not explicitly codified in Iran's Penal Code but is a capital offense under Islamic jurisprudence applied by Iranian courts. Male apostates can be sentenced to death; female apostates may receive life imprisonment. The crime of 'insulting Islam' (blasphemy) carries similar penalties. These laws are used against converts to Christianity and other religions. Several individuals have been executed for apostasy-related charges. International pressure has led some sentences to be commuted.
laws.penalty: Death penalty for male apostates; imprisonment or death for female apostates; based on judicial interpretation of Islamic law
exceptions: Diplomatic pressure occasionally leads to commutation
Some apostasy charges folded into broader 'national security' charges
laws.source: Iranian Islamic Jurisprudence applied through courts; Islamic Penal Code

quiz.q: How does Iranian law treat male apostasy (leaving Islam)?
options: A civil matter with no criminal penalty
A social stigma but not a crime
A potentially capital offense under Islamic jurisprudence
quiz.explanation: Male apostasy (leaving Islam) is treated as a potentially capital offense under Islamic jurisprudence applied by Iranian courts, despite not being explicitly codified, and can result in a death sentence for conversion to another religion.

laws.title: Oil and Gas — National Control
laws.subtitle: Nationalized petroleum industry under sanctions
laws.fullDescription: Iran's petroleum industry is nationalized under the National Iranian Oil Company (NIOC). Oil and gas are central to the Iranian economy, representing a major portion of government revenue. International sanctions have severely limited Iran's oil exports, forcing Iran to find workarounds including selling oil to China through informal channels and using shadow tanker fleets. The Petroleum Law governs upstream oil and gas activities. Iran holds the world's second-largest natural gas reserves and fourth-largest oil reserves.
laws.penalty: Criminal penalties for unauthorized oil trading or sanctions evasion assistance
exceptions: Domestic petroleum consumption not affected by export sanctions
Humanitarian exceptions theoretically exist for oil-for-food arrangements
laws.source: Iranian Petroleum Law; National Iranian Oil Company Statute

quiz.q: What is Iran's status regarding world oil and gas reserves?
options: Second-largest oil reserves, largest gas reserves
Second-largest natural gas reserves and fourth-largest oil reserves
Largest combined reserves in the world
quiz.explanation: Iran holds the world's second-largest natural gas reserves (after Russia) and the fourth-largest crude oil reserves, making it an energy-rich nation whose petroleum exports have been severely restricted by international sanctions.

laws.title: Drug Trafficking — Mandatory Death Penalty
laws.subtitle: Execution for drug offenses
laws.fullDescription: Iran has historically imposed the death penalty for drug trafficking, and drug offenses account for a significant proportion of executions. The 2017 anti-narcotics law reform raised the threshold for mandatory death sentences from 30g to 2kg for heroin/morphine, reducing (but not eliminating) executions for drug offenses. Iran argues it is on the front line of combating drug trafficking from Afghanistan, which is the world's largest opium producer. Drug addiction is a major public health problem in Iran.
laws.penalty: Death penalty for trafficking above threshold amounts; imprisonment for smaller quantities
exceptions: 2017 reform raised thresholds, converting many death sentences to imprisonment
Addiction treatment programs available for drug users
laws.source: Iranian Anti-Narcotics Law (revised 2017)

quiz.q: What reform did Iran make to its drug trafficking death penalty law in 2017?
options: Abolished the death penalty for all drug offenses
Increased executions for all drug offenses
Raised the threshold from 30g to 2kg, reducing but not eliminating drug-related executions
quiz.explanation: Iran's 2017 anti-narcotics law reform raised the threshold for mandatory death sentences from 30g to 2kg for heroin/morphine, which significantly reduced (but did not eliminate) the number of drug-related executions.

laws.title: Defamation of the Supreme Leader
laws.subtitle: Insulting senior officials is a criminal offense
laws.fullDescription: Insulting or defaming the Supreme Leader, President, or other senior government officials is a criminal offense in Iran carrying severe penalties. Criticism of the political system is treated as a national security offense. Social media posts critical of officials have led to arrests and prosecution. The charge of 'propaganda against the state' is frequently used against journalists, activists, and ordinary citizens who post critical content online. Dual nationals and foreign journalists have been arrested for such offenses.
laws.penalty: Imprisonment 1-10 years for insulting the Supreme Leader; flogging and imprisonment for state propaganda
exceptions: Approved criticism within official channels is permitted
Academic and theological debate within approved frameworks
laws.source: Iranian Islamic Penal Code, Articles 514-515; Press Law

quiz.q: What charge is frequently used against journalists and citizens who post critical content about Iran's government online?
quiz.explanation: The charge of 'propaganda against the state' is frequently used against journalists, activists, and ordinary citizens in Iran for posting critical content online, making it one of the most commonly used charges against political dissidents.

laws.title: Labor Code — Workers' Rights Under Islamic Law
laws.subtitle: Formal labor protections with significant restrictions
laws.fullDescription: Iran's Labor Law (1990) establishes workers' rights including maximum working hours (44 hours/week), annual leave, and safety standards. Independent trade unions are not permitted — only the state-sanctioned Islamic Labour Councils are allowed. Strikes are generally prohibited. Labor disputes are handled through Islamic Labour Councils and the Ministry of Labour. Workers protesting for wages have faced arrest. Teachers' and truck drivers' strikes have been suppressed.
laws.penalty: Criminal charges for organizing independent unions or unauthorized strikes
exceptions: Islamic Labour Councils are legal and permitted
Workers can petition Ministry of Labour for dispute resolution
laws.source: Iranian Labour Law, 1990

quiz.q: What type of trade unions are prohibited in Iran?
options: Independent trade unions (only state-sanctioned Islamic Labour Councils permitted)
quiz.explanation: Independent trade unions are prohibited in Iran; only state-sanctioned Islamic Labour Councils are permitted, and strikes are generally illegal. Workers who organize independently face arrest and prosecution.

laws.title: Espionage and National Security Law
laws.subtitle: Broad security laws used against dual nationals
laws.fullDescription: Iran's laws on espionage and national security are extremely broad and have been used to arrest and imprison foreign nationals, dual nationals, journalists, and academics visiting Iran. Iran does not recognize dual nationality, meaning dual citizens arrested in Iran are treated as Iranian nationals without consular access from their other country. The 'hostage diplomacy' or 'detention diplomacy' practice — arresting foreign nationals for bargaining leverage — has been widely documented. Several Western citizens remain detained.
laws.penalty: Imprisonment 1-15 years for espionage; death penalty for espionage against national security
exceptions: Iran does not recognize dual nationality, so second citizenship provides no legal protection
Diplomatic negotiations sometimes lead to prisoner exchanges
laws.source: Iranian Islamic Penal Code, Articles 501-515
laws.sourceLabel: Iranian Espionage and National Security Law

quiz.q: Why do dual nationals arrested in Iran receive no consular protection from their second country?
options: Iran has no diplomatic relations with other countries
International law does not require consular access
Iran does not recognize dual nationality, treating dual citizens as solely Iranian
Dual nationals voluntarily waive consular rights
quiz.explanation: Iran does not recognize dual nationality, so dual citizens arrested in Iran are treated as solely Iranian nationals. This means they cannot receive consular assistance from their other country, leaving them without the diplomatic protection normally afforded to foreign nationals.

laws.title: Banking Law — Interest Prohibition
laws.subtitle: Islamic banking with interest-free system
laws.fullDescription: Iran's Banking Law (1983) prohibits interest (riba), implementing Islamic banking principles throughout the entire financial system. Banks operate on profit-sharing, leasing, and fee-based transactions rather than interest. Iran has one of the world's few entirely Islamic banking systems (as opposed to individual Islamic windows within conventional banks). The system has been criticized for inefficiency and for effectively charging interest under different names. International sanctions have further complicated banking operations.
laws.penalty: Criminal penalties for charging conventional interest (riba)
exceptions: Government bonds use profit-sharing certificates rather than interest
Foreign bank branches theoretically exempt but largely excluded due to sanctions
laws.source: Iranian Law on Usury-Free Banking, 1983

quiz.q: What year did Iran implement its prohibition on banking interest under Islamic banking law?
quiz.explanation: Iran implemented the Law on Usury-Free Banking in 1983, making Iran one of the very few countries in the world to implement Islamic banking principles across its entire financial system, prohibiting conventional interest (riba) throughout.

laws.title: Mahsa Amini Protests — Legal Aftermath
laws.subtitle: 2022 Woman, Life, Freedom movement and government response
laws.fullDescription: The September 2022 death of Mahsa (Zhina) Amini in morality police custody triggered nationwide protests known as the Woman, Life, Freedom movement. The government's response included the killing of an estimated 500+ protesters, mass arrests of 15,000+, and the execution of at least 9 protesters on moharebeh and 'corruption on earth' charges. The protests were the most significant challenge to the Islamic Republic since 1979. New mandatory hijab enforcement laws were passed in 2023 in response.
laws.penalty: Death penalty applied to protest leaders on moharebeh charges; imprisonment for most protesters
exceptions: International pressure led to some releases
Cases of minors handled separately in juvenile courts
laws.source: Various Iranian Penal Code provisions applied to 2022-2023 protests

quiz.q: What was the estimated number of protesters killed during Iran's 2022 Woman, Life, Freedom protests?
quiz.explanation: Estimates suggest over 500 protesters were killed during Iran's 2022 Woman, Life, Freedom movement, with approximately 15,000+ arrested. At least 9 protesters were executed on moharebeh charges in the following months.

laws.title: Lake Urmia — Environmental Crisis Law
laws.subtitle: Shrinking inland lake and environmental policy failures
laws.fullDescription: Lake Urmia in northwestern Iran was once the world's third-largest saltwater lake. It has lost over 90% of its water volume due to agricultural water diversion, climate change, and dam construction. The Iranian government has invested billions in restoration but with limited success. The lake's shrinkage has created salt dust storms affecting millions of people in the region. Environmental law and agricultural water use policy failures contributed to the crisis. The Lake Urmia Restoration Program involves multiple agencies.
laws.penalty: Agricultural water use violations subject to fines and license revocation
exceptions: Existing agricultural water rights difficult to revoke
Emergency drought provisions affect enforcement
laws.source: Iranian Environmental Protection Organization; Lake Urmia Restoration Program

quiz.q: How much water volume has Lake Urmia lost?
quiz.explanation: Lake Urmia has lost over 90% of its water volume due to agricultural water diversion, dam construction, and climate change, transforming from the world's third-largest saltwater lake into a fraction of its former size.

laws.title: Child Marriage — Legal Minimum Ages
laws.subtitle: Low minimum marriage age enables child marriage
laws.fullDescription: Iran's Civil Code sets the minimum age for marriage at 13 for girls and 15 for boys, with a judge's permission allowing marriage at even younger ages. Iran has one of the world's highest rates of child marriage, with an estimated 17% of girls married before age 18 in rural areas (and much higher in some provinces). International organizations have repeatedly called for Iran to raise the minimum marriage age to 18. The 2013 Penal Code reforms did not address child marriage.
laws.penalty: Criminal penalties for non-compliance with minimum age requirements, but enforcement is weak
exceptions: Judicial permission allows marriages below the standard minimum ages
Customary tribal marriages in rural areas often go unregistered
laws.source: Iranian Civil Code, Article 1041

quiz.q: What percentage of girls in rural Iran are estimated to marry before age 18?
quiz.explanation: An estimated 17% of girls in rural Iran (and significantly more in some provinces) marry before age 18, a rate that has drawn international criticism given Iran's minimum marriage age of 13 for girls under the Civil Code.

laws.title: Political Prisoners
laws.subtitle: Mass detention of dissidents, journalists, and activists
laws.fullDescription: Iran holds thousands of political prisoners including journalists, human rights defenders, ethnic minority activists, labor organizers, environmental activists, and dual nationals. The 1988 prison massacres, in which thousands of political prisoners were executed on orders attributed to Ayatollah Khomeini, remain an unacknowledged atrocity. The UN Special Rapporteur on Iran regularly documents political detention. Evin Prison in Tehran is the main detention facility for political prisoners. Torture in detention has been extensively documented.
laws.penalty: Sentences range from months to life imprisonment; death penalty applied in some cases
exceptions: Diplomatic pressure occasionally leads to temporary releases or medical furloughs
International prisoner exchanges have released some dual nationals
laws.source: Iranian law as applied; UN Special Rapporteur on Human Rights in Iran

quiz.q: What is the name of Tehran's main prison for political detainees?
quiz.explanation: Evin Prison in Tehran is Iran's main facility for political prisoners, journalists, activists, and dual nationals. It has become internationally synonymous with political detention in Iran.

laws.title: Ethnic Minorities — Kurdish, Arab, Baloch Rights
laws.subtitle: Persecution of non-Persian ethnic minorities
laws.fullDescription: Iran's non-Persian ethnic minorities (Kurds, Arabs in Khuzestan, Baloch, Azeris, and Turkmen) face discrimination in language, culture, and political representation. The constitution designates Persian as the official language, limiting minority language education. Kurdish political groups (KDPI, Komala) are designated as terrorist organizations. Arab separatism in Khuzestan is suppressed. Balochistan faces military operations against Baloch militant groups. Ethnic minority activists face disproportionate death sentences.
laws.penalty: Death penalty applied disproportionately to ethnic minority activists
exceptions: Some minority cultural expression permitted in designated spaces
Azerbaijani Iranians have somewhat more latitude given their size
laws.source: Iranian Constitution, Article 15; Islamic Penal Code applications

quiz.q: Which ethnic minority regions of Iran face particular military operations and suppression?
quiz.explanation: Iran's Balochistan and Kurdish regions face particular military operations and security suppression, with Kurdish and Baloch activists facing disproportionate death sentences and their political organizations designated as terrorist groups.

laws.title: Economic Mismanagement and Inflation
laws.subtitle: Hyperinflation and economic crisis under sanctions
laws.fullDescription: Iran's economy has faced severe challenges from international sanctions, government mismanagement, and corruption. The Iranian rial has lost over 90% of its value against the dollar since 2018. Inflation has regularly exceeded 40-50% annually. Iran's Revolutionary Guards (IRGC) controls an estimated 30-40% of the economy through affiliated companies, creating conflicts of interest. Fuel and food subsidies have attempted to cushion impacts on the poor but have been inadequately funded.
laws.penalty: Criminal penalties for economic crimes and currency violations
exceptions: IRGC-affiliated businesses operate with preferential treatment
State companies exempt from some competition rules
laws.source: Central Bank of Iran; Iranian Economic Data

quiz.q: What percentage of Iran's economy is estimated to be controlled by the Revolutionary Guards (IRGC)?
quiz.explanation: Iran's Revolutionary Guards (IRGC) controls an estimated 30-40% of Iran's economy through affiliated companies and foundations, creating significant conflicts of interest in policymaking and economic governance.

laws.title: Solitary Confinement and Torture
laws.subtitle: Documented use of torture in Iranian detention
laws.fullDescription: The UN Committee Against Torture and numerous human rights organizations have extensively documented the use of torture in Iranian detention facilities. Methods include prolonged solitary confinement, sleep deprivation, mock executions, beatings, and psychological torture. 'White torture' — prolonged sensory deprivation through solitary confinement — has been used against political detainees. Iran ratified the UN Convention Against Torture but has been repeatedly found in violation of its obligations.
laws.penalty: N/A — torture is illegal under Iranian law in principle but widely practiced
exceptions: Iran disputes most torture allegations
Security forces have broad immunity in practice
laws.source: UN CAT Reports on Iran; Amnesty International, Human Rights Watch documentation

quiz.q: What is 'white torture' as practiced in Iranian prisons?
options: Use of chemical substances during interrogation
Prolonged sensory deprivation through solitary confinement
quiz.explanation: 'White torture' refers to prolonged sensory deprivation through solitary confinement in white-painted cells, with minimal sensory stimulation, used against political detainees in Iran. It causes severe psychological damage.

laws.title: Guardian Council — Election Vetting
laws.subtitle: Clerical body vets all electoral candidates
laws.fullDescription: Iran's Guardian Council, composed of 6 Islamic jurists appointed by the Supreme Leader and 6 lawyers approved by Parliament, vets all candidates for presidential, parliamentary, and Assembly of Experts elections. The Council can disqualify candidates it considers insufficiently Islamic or disloyal to the system (Velayat-e Faqih). Mass disqualifications have limited genuine competition — thousands of parliamentary candidates are rejected in each election cycle. In 2021, most reformist presidential candidates were disqualified.
laws.penalty: N/A — constitutional electoral process
exceptions: Approved reformists can participate within the system
Some moderate candidates occasionally approved to maintain appearance of competition
laws.source: Iranian Constitution, Article 91-99; Electoral Laws

quiz.q: How many Islamic jurists appointed by the Supreme Leader sit on Iran's Guardian Council?
quiz.explanation: Iran's Guardian Council consists of 12 members: 6 Islamic jurists appointed by the Supreme Leader and 6 lawyers approved by Parliament. The 6 Supreme Leader-appointed jurists give him significant influence over the Council's decisions.

laws.title: Air Pollution — Tehran's Crisis
laws.subtitle: Severe urban air pollution affecting millions
laws.fullDescription: Tehran regularly experiences dangerously high air pollution levels, with schools and businesses closing during pollution peaks. The main causes are vehicle emissions (a large fleet of old, poorly maintained vehicles), industrial pollution, topographic trapping of pollutants in the Tehran bowl, and domestic heating. Iran has policies to replace old vehicles and improve fuel standards, but implementation has been hampered by sanctions on imported car parts and fuel quality issues. Deaths from air pollution are estimated in the tens of thousands annually.
laws.penalty: Industrial emissions violations subject to fines; vehicle emissions standards enforced
exceptions: Agricultural burning in surrounding provinces contributes to pollution outside direct city control
Emergency closures ordered by government during extreme events
laws.source: Iranian Department of Environment; Tehran Air Quality Control Company

quiz.q: What geographic feature contributes to Tehran's severe air pollution?
options: The Tehran bowl — topographic trapping of pollutants
Prevailing westerly winds carrying Saharan dust
Dense forest burning in surrounding hills
quiz.explanation: Tehran's bowl-shaped geographic location — surrounded by mountains — traps pollutants from vehicle emissions and industry, preventing dispersal and contributing to the city's chronic air quality crisis.

laws.title: Propaganda Against the State
laws.subtitle: Criminal offense for criticizing the government
laws.fullDescription: Article 500 of Iran's Islamic Penal Code criminalizes 'propaganda against the Islamic Republic.' This broadly interpreted offense covers writings, speeches, social media posts, interviews with foreign media, and participation in peaceful protests that are deemed critical of the government. The charge is used routinely against journalists, bloggers, academics, lawyers, and activists. Possession of banned literature or VPN software can contribute to such charges.
laws.penalty: Imprisonment 3 months to 1 year for first offense; up to 5 years for repeated or aggravated cases
exceptions: Approved criticism within state media and official channels is permitted
Academic publications within approved topics
laws.source: Iranian Islamic Penal Code, Article 500

quiz.q: What activities can constitute 'propaganda against the state' under Article 500 of Iran's Penal Code?
options: Writings, social media posts, interviews with foreign media, and peaceful protest
quiz.explanation: Article 500's broad interpretation covers writings, social media posts, interviews with foreign media, and peaceful protests critical of the government, making it a sweeping tool for suppressing political dissent.

laws.title: Child Custody — Father's Automatic Rights
laws.subtitle: Fathers receive custody at set ages
laws.fullDescription: Under Iranian family law, custody of children after divorce is determined by the child's age: the mother has custody of daughters until age 7 and sons until age 2, after which custody automatically transfers to the father. This rule applies regardless of the father's fitness. After puberty, children can choose their custodial parent. The grandmother (paternal) gets custody if the father is deceased. These rules have been criticized as prioritizing patriarchal rights over children's best interests.
laws.penalty: Criminal penalties for violating court custody orders
exceptions: Courts can award mother custody in cases of proven parental unfitness
Post-puberty children can choose their custodial parent
laws.source: Iranian Civil Code, Articles 1169-1174

quiz.q: At what age does custody of sons automatically transfer from mother to father in Iran?
quiz.explanation: Under Iranian law, custody of sons automatically transfers to the father at age 2 (and daughters at age 7), regardless of the father's fitness as a parent — a rule criticized for prioritizing patriarchal rights over children's best interests.

laws.title: Assembly of Experts — Supervision of Supreme Leader
laws.subtitle: Clerical body that theoretically oversees Supreme Leader
laws.fullDescription: Iran's Assembly of Experts is an 88-member body of Islamic jurists elected every 8 years (but candidates vetted by the Guardian Council). The Assembly has the constitutional authority to appoint, supervise, and potentially remove the Supreme Leader. In practice, the Assembly has never challenged any Supreme Leader and is widely seen as subservient to the Leader rather than supervising him. The Guardian Council's vetting ensures only loyalists are elected to the Assembly.
laws.penalty: N/A — constitutional body
exceptions: Assembly of Experts theoretically has supervisory power but has never exercised it
Constitutional provisions for dismissal of Supreme Leader never invoked
laws.source: Iranian Constitution, Articles 107-111

quiz.q: What theoretical power does Iran's Assembly of Experts have that it has never exercised?
options: Appoint, supervise, and potentially remove the Supreme Leader
quiz.explanation: Iran's Assembly of Experts has the constitutional authority to appoint, supervise, and potentially remove the Supreme Leader, but has never exercised its supervisory role, being composed of clerics loyal to the Supreme Leader.

laws.title: Revolutionary Guards Economic Empire
laws.subtitle: IRGC controls vast economic interests
laws.fullDescription: The Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC) controls an estimated 30-40% of Iran's economy through holding companies including Khatam al-Anbiya construction company (which has received billions in no-bid contracts), media companies, and businesses in telecommunications, oil, and banking. IRGC-affiliated entities are exempt from many regulations and receive preferential treatment in government procurement. This economic power reinforces the IRGC's political independence from elected government. The IRGC has been designated a terrorist organization by the US.
laws.penalty: N/A — IRGC operates with preferential legal status
exceptions: IRGC entities exempt from standard procurement competition
IRGC operations classified as national security matters
laws.source: Various Iranian economic and government sources; US Treasury IRGC designations

quiz.q: What is the name of the IRGC's main construction and engineering company?
quiz.explanation: Khatam al-Anbiya is the IRGC's main construction and engineering company, which has received billions in no-bid government contracts for major infrastructure projects including dams, pipelines, and urban development.

laws.title: Dual Nationals — Hostage Diplomacy
laws.subtitle: Foreign and dual nationals used as diplomatic bargaining chips
laws.fullDescription: Iran has a documented practice of arresting dual nationals and foreign nationals on broad espionage or security charges, which critics call 'hostage diplomacy' or 'arbitrary detention.' Those arrested are often held in Evin Prison's Ward 209 (Intelligence Ministry ward). Arrests frequently coincide with diplomatic tensions with the detainee's home country. Several high-profile cases have involved American, British, French, German, Swedish, and other Western citizens. Some have been exchanged in prisoner swaps.
laws.penalty: Imprisonment typically 5-15 years; death penalty possible
exceptions: Prisoner exchanges have led to some releases
International pressure sometimes leads to medical releases
laws.source: Various documented cases; UN Working Group on Arbitrary Detention

quiz.q: What specific prison ward in Iran holds most dual national and foreign detainees?
options: Ward 209 (Intelligence Ministry Ward in Evin Prison)
quiz.explanation: Ward 209 of Evin Prison, managed by the Intelligence Ministry, is where most dual nationals and foreign detainees are held in Iran, often in solitary confinement for extended periods during interrogation.

laws.title: Higher Education — Political Controls
laws.subtitle: University admissions and academic freedom restrictions
laws.fullDescription: Iran's universities are state-controlled, with admissions through the Konkur (university entrance exam) system. Following the 1979 revolution, the 'Cultural Revolution' closed universities for 3 years to Islamicize curricula. Today, political vetting affects faculty appointments and some student admissions. Bahá'ís are systematically banned from university education. Women face restrictions in some fields. Political activity by students is monitored and suppressed. Academic freedom is significantly restricted.
laws.penalty: Expulsion for political activity; faculty dismissal for deviation from approved ideology
exceptions: Sciences and engineering have relatively more academic freedom
Private universities have somewhat more flexibility in some areas
laws.source: Iranian Higher Education Council; Cultural Revolution policies

quiz.q: Which religious group is systematically banned from attending Iranian universities?
quiz.explanation: Bahá'ís are systematically excluded from Iranian universities, as the government refuses to recognize Bahá'í as a legitimate religion and actively denies Bahá'ís access to higher education as a form of religious persecution.

laws.title: IRGC Terrorism Designation
laws.subtitle: International consequences of IRGC activities
laws.fullDescription: The US designated the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC) as a Foreign Terrorist Organization (FTO) in 2019 — the first time a government military force was so designated. The IRGC and its overseas operations arm, the Quds Force, have been involved in proxy conflicts in Syria, Iraq, Lebanon (Hezbollah), Yemen (Houthis), and Gaza (Hamas support). IRGC commanders have been targeted in US drone strikes, including the killing of General Qasem Soleimani in January 2020. These designations affect Iran's international relationships and economy.
laws.penalty: Criminal penalties under US law for materially supporting the IRGC
exceptions: Diplomatic communications between countries not technically affected by designation
Humanitarian work not directly supporting IRGC activities
laws.source: US FTO Designation 2019; IRGC Activities Documentation

quiz.q: What was historically significant about the US designation of Iran's IRGC as a Foreign Terrorist Organization in 2019?
options: First time a Middle Eastern military force was designated
First time any military force of a recognized government was so designated
First time multiple countries jointly designated a group
First time a nuclear power's military was designated
quiz.explanation: The US designation of Iran's IRGC as a Foreign Terrorist Organization in 2019 was historically significant as the first time any military force of a recognized government had been designated as a foreign terrorist organization by the United States.

laws.title: Water Crisis — Droughts and Mismanagement
laws.subtitle: Severe water scarcity threatening multiple regions
laws.fullDescription: Iran faces a severe water crisis driven by climate change, agricultural overuse, dam construction, and population growth. Multiple provinces face acute water shortages. Protests over water scarcity have occurred in Khuzestan (2021) and Isfahan (2021-2022). The drying of rivers including the Zayandeh Rud in Isfahan has destroyed livelihoods. Iran's agricultural sector uses about 90% of water resources, primarily through inefficient flood irrigation. Government responses have focused on water transfer projects rather than efficiency improvements.
laws.penalty: Fines for unauthorized water extraction; agricultural water rights can be revoked
exceptions: Historical water rights difficult to revoke despite inefficiency
Emergency drought allocations can override normal licensing
laws.source: Iranian Water Resource Management; Environmental Protection Organization

quiz.q: What percentage of Iran's water resources does the agricultural sector consume?
quiz.explanation: Iran's agricultural sector consumes approximately 90% of the country's water resources, primarily through inefficient flood irrigation methods, making agriculture the central challenge in addressing Iran's severe water crisis.

laws.title: Baha'i Persecution — Systematic Discrimination
laws.subtitle: Bahá'í minority faces systematic legal discrimination
laws.fullDescription: Iran's approximately 300,000 Bahá'ís face systematic legal discrimination. The Bahá'í Faith is not recognized as a religion under Iranian law (the constitution only recognizes Islam, Christianity, Judaism, and Zoroastrianism). Bahá'ís cannot practice their religion, run their own schools, or attend university. Bahá'í marriages are not legally recognized, depriving them of inheritance and other rights. Leaders of the Yaran (Bahá'í leadership group) have been repeatedly arrested and imprisoned on spurious charges.
laws.penalty: Imprisonment for practicing Bahá'í faith; denial of government employment and education
exceptions: Individual Bahá'ís may convert to Islam to access rights
Some private activities tolerated in practice but still illegal
laws.source: Iranian Constitution; Islamic Penal Code applications to Bahá'ís

quiz.q: What is the estimated Bahá'í population in Iran that faces systematic discrimination?
quiz.explanation: Iran has an estimated 300,000 Bahá'ís who face systematic legal discrimination including exclusion from universities, unrecognized marriages, prohibition on religious practice, and regular imprisonment of community leaders.

laws.title: Expediency Council — Arbitrator
laws.subtitle: Body that resolves disputes between parliament and Guardian Council
laws.fullDescription: The Expediency Council (Majma' Tashkhis-e Maslahat-e Nezam) was created in 1988 to resolve disputes between parliament and the Guardian Council. When parliament passes legislation the Guardian Council rejects as un-Islamic, the Expediency Council arbitrates. The Council also advises the Supreme Leader on policy. Its members are appointed by the Supreme Leader for 5-year terms. The Council represents a pragmatic element in Iran's system, allowing consideration of state interests alongside strict Islamic law.
laws.penalty: N/A — constitutional consultative body
exceptions: Decisions are binding on parliament and Guardian Council
Supreme Leader can override Expediency Council decisions
laws.source: Iranian Constitution, Article 112; 1989 Constitutional Revision

quiz.q: When was Iran's Expediency Council created?
quiz.explanation: The Expediency Council was created in 1988 to resolve legislative disputes between parliament and the Guardian Council, and was formally incorporated into the constitution during the 1989 revision under Ayatollah Khamenei.

laws.title: Agricultural Workers — Rural Economy
laws.subtitle: Rural livelihoods under economic pressure
laws.fullDescription: Iran's rural agricultural sector employs approximately 18% of the workforce. Smallholder farmers face challenges from water scarcity, rural-urban migration, and competition from imported goods (despite official subsidies). The government subsidizes key agricultural inputs. Land reform in the 1980s distributed some land but the sector remains relatively inefficient. Agricultural workers have fewer formal labor protections than urban industrial workers. Rural poverty is significantly higher than urban poverty.
laws.penalty: N/A — agricultural labor regulation
exceptions: Agricultural subsidies modify market outcomes
Cooperative farming receives preferential credit
laws.source: Iranian Ministry of Agriculture; Labor Statistics

quiz.q: What percentage of Iran's workforce is employed in agriculture?
quiz.explanation: Approximately 18% of Iran's workforce is employed in agriculture, a sector facing significant challenges from water scarcity, rural-urban migration, and economic pressures including sanctions effects on imported inputs.

laws.title: Foreign Policy — Regional Proxy Networks
laws.subtitle: Legal framework for Iran's regional interventions
laws.fullDescription: Iran's IRGC Quds Force manages a network of proxy forces across the Middle East including Hezbollah in Lebanon, Hamas in Gaza, the Houthis in Yemen, and various Iraqi militias. These activities, while considered by Iran as legitimate support for resistance movements, are treated as terrorism by Western governments. Iranian law criminalizes opposition to these activities as 'treason.' The Quds Force commander operates outside normal civil law accountability. Iran's regional strategy is constitutional foreign policy implemented through military means.
laws.penalty: Treason charges for opposing IRGC regional activities; domestic opposition suppressed
exceptions: Approved political debate about foreign policy within limits permitted
Diplomatic staff operate under standard diplomatic immunity abroad
laws.source: Iranian Constitution, Articles 152-155; IRGC organizational law
laws.sourceLabel: IRGC Quds Force and Regional Policy

quiz.q: What is the name of the IRGC's overseas operations arm that manages Iran's proxy networks?
quiz.explanation: The Quds Force (also spelled Al-Quds Force) is the IRGC's overseas operations arm responsible for managing Iran's proxy networks including Hezbollah, Hamas support, Houthi assistance, and Iraqi militias.

laws.title: Healthcare System — Universal Coverage
laws.subtitle: National health insurance and public healthcare
laws.fullDescription: Iran has made significant progress in healthcare access since the 1979 revolution. The Health Transformation Plan (2014) expanded insurance coverage and reduced out-of-pocket payments. Iran has achieved near-universal healthcare coverage and has good health indicators compared to regional peers. Medical education is strong, and Iran has a well-developed pharmaceutical industry. International sanctions have affected access to medicines and medical equipment, creating shortages of specialized drugs.
laws.penalty: N/A — healthcare policy
exceptions: Private healthcare available for those who can afford it
International emergency medical assistance has some sanctions exemptions
laws.source: Iranian Ministry of Health; Health Transformation Plan

quiz.q: What plan expanded Iran's healthcare coverage and reduced out-of-pocket payments?
quiz.explanation: Iran's Health Transformation Plan, launched in 2014, significantly expanded insurance coverage, reduced out-of-pocket payments for hospital services, and aimed at near-universal healthcare coverage, building on existing health infrastructure.

laws.title: Cultural Restrictions — Music, Film, Art
laws.subtitle: State control of cultural production
laws.fullDescription: Iran's Ministry of Culture and Islamic Guidance (Ershad) must approve all films, music, books, and cultural events. Western music is restricted but Persian pop music is regulated rather than banned. Iranian cinema has achieved international acclaim within these constraints (Abbas Kiarostami, Asghar Farhadi). Concerts by female solo performers are restricted or banned. Certain topics (LGBTQ+ themes, extramarital relationships, alcohol) cannot be depicted. Satellite dishes (for receiving foreign TV) are illegal but widely tolerated.
laws.penalty: Criminal penalties for producing or distributing uncensored cultural content
exceptions: Some satellite dish possession is tolerated in practice
Underground art scenes operate with some de facto tolerance
Iranian cinema receives selective international exhibition rights
laws.source: Iranian Ministry of Culture and Islamic Guidance regulations
laws.sourceLabel: Ministry of Culture and Islamic Guidance Controls

quiz.q: What has Iran's cinema industry achieved despite extensive state censorship?
options: International acclaim with filmmakers like Asghar Farhadi winning Academy Awards
Only documentaries approved for international festivals
Banned from all international film festivals
quiz.explanation: Despite extensive state censorship, Iranian cinema has achieved remarkable international acclaim, with directors like Asghar Farhadi winning Academy Awards (for 'A Separation' and 'The Salesman') and Abbas Kiarostami winning the Palme d'Or at Cannes.

laws.title: Basij — Paramilitary Enforcement
laws.subtitle: Volunteer paramilitary forces enforcing social laws
laws.fullDescription: The Basij (Mobilization Resistance Force) is a paramilitary volunteer organization under IRGC command. The Basij enforces social and moral laws, suppresses protests, and acts as a parallel security force. During the 2022 protests, Basij forces were responsible for many killings of protesters. The Basij has an estimated 90,000 active members and a much larger reserve force. Members receive economic benefits including preferential access to housing, employment, and university admissions.
laws.penalty: Basij members act as de facto law enforcement; victims of Basij violence rarely get justice
exceptions: Basij members have broad immunity for actions taken 'in service'
Basij operates outside normal police accountability mechanisms
laws.source: Iranian Constitution; IRGC Organizational Law

quiz.q: What benefits do Basij members receive that create incentives for joining?
options: Preferential access to housing, employment, and university admissions
quiz.explanation: Basij members receive significant economic benefits including preferential access to housing, employment, and university admissions, creating material incentives for joining that help maintain the force's size.

laws.title: Bonyads — Religious Foundations
laws.subtitle: Tax-exempt religious foundations controlling vast wealth
laws.fullDescription: Bonyads (religious foundations) are semi-state organizations originally established with assets confiscated after the 1979 revolution. Major bonyads include the Bonyad Mostazafin (Foundation of the Oppressed), Astan Quds Razavi (Imam Reza shrine foundation), and Bonyad Shahid (Martyrs Foundation). They control an estimated 20-30% of Iran's non-oil economy. Bonyads are largely exempt from taxes and oversight, and their accounts are not publicly disclosed. They are closely linked to the Supreme Leader's office.
laws.penalty: N/A — bonyads operate with special legal status exempt from normal oversight
exceptions: Bonyads are exempt from standard tax and transparency requirements
Not subject to normal corporate governance
laws.source: Iranian Constitutional Law; Bonyad organizational laws

quiz.q: Approximately what percentage of Iran's non-oil economy do Bonyads control?
quiz.explanation: Iran's Bonyads (religious foundations) control an estimated 20-30% of the non-oil economy, operating largely tax-free and without public transparency, with their accounts not subject to standard oversight.

laws.title: Weapons Development — Chemical/Nuclear Programs
laws.subtitle: Iran's weapons programs and international law
laws.fullDescription: Iran's nuclear program has been a source of international tension since the early 2000s. Iran maintains it has the right to peaceful nuclear development under the Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT). The IAEA has documented Iranian activities inconsistent with civilian use. Iran had a documented chemical weapons program (used against Kurdish civilians in the 1980s Iraq-Iran War). Iran is a party to the Chemical Weapons Convention. The JCPOA nuclear deal (2015-2018) provided a framework limiting enrichment, which Iran has progressively violated since the US withdrawal.
laws.penalty: N/A — state weapons programs; individuals assisting weapons proliferation face international sanctions
exceptions: Domestic Iranian law supports nuclear development as sovereign right
Chemical weapons development was historical; current CWC compliance claimed
laws.source: IAEA Reports on Iran; Chemical Weapons Convention; NPT

quiz.q: What does Iran maintain regarding its right to nuclear development under international law?
options: Iran has no legal right to any nuclear activities
Iran has the right to peaceful nuclear development under the Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT)
Iran only needs IAEA permission for each specific activity
Iran has withdrawn from the NPT
quiz.explanation: Iran maintains that it has the right to peaceful nuclear development, including uranium enrichment, under the Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT) as a signatory, while the IAEA has documented activities inconsistent with purely civilian purposes.

laws.title: Refugee and Asylum Policy
laws.subtitle: Iran hosts large Afghan refugee population
laws.fullDescription: Iran hosts one of the world's largest refugee populations — an estimated 3-4 million Afghans (registered and unregistered), making it the world's second-largest refugee-hosting country after Turkey. Many Afghans have been in Iran for decades following the Soviet invasion and subsequent conflicts. Iran has periodically deported large numbers of Afghans. Registered refugees have some access to education and healthcare, but face discrimination. Following the Taliban takeover in 2021, refugee flows increased significantly.
laws.penalty: Criminal penalties for illegal residence; deportation without due process for unregistered Afghans
exceptions: UNHCR-registered refugees have some protection
Long-term residents may qualify for extended stay permits
laws.source: Iranian Law on Entry and Residence of Foreigners; UNHCR Iran Reports

quiz.q: How many Afghans (registered and unregistered) are estimated to be in Iran?
quiz.explanation: Iran hosts an estimated 3-4 million Afghans (registered and unregistered), making it the world's second-largest refugee-hosting country, a population that has been in Iran for decades across multiple waves of conflict-driven displacement.

laws.title: Execution of Juvenile Offenders
laws.subtitle: Death sentences for crimes committed as minors
laws.fullDescription: Despite the 2013 Islamic Penal Code reforms that introduced provisions allowing judges to order psychological evaluation instead of execution for juvenile offenders, Iran continues to execute people for crimes committed when they were minors. Iran is one of the few countries in the world that executes juvenile offenders (alongside Saudi Arabia and a few others). Several individuals have been executed after spending years on death row for crimes committed before age 18. International human rights law absolutely prohibits execution of juvenile offenders.
laws.penalty: Death penalty applied despite protections theoretically existing for juvenile offenders
exceptions: 2013 reforms allow psychological evaluation that may substitute for execution
International pressure has led to some commutations
laws.source: Iranian Islamic Penal Code, 2013; Amnesty International Reports

quiz.q: What does international human rights law say about executing juvenile offenders?
options: Allows it for heinous crimes only
quiz.explanation: International human rights law, including the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child and the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, absolutely prohibits the execution of persons for offenses committed when they were under 18 years of age.

laws.title: Persian Gulf — Environmental Threats
laws.subtitle: Marine environment degradation in the Persian Gulf
laws.fullDescription: The Persian Gulf, which Iran borders for over 1,700 km, faces severe environmental threats including oil spills, industrial discharge, desalination brine, and coral reef bleaching. Iran's offshore oil operations have contributed to pollution. The IRGC's commercial activities in the Gulf include smuggling networks that contribute to illegal trade and environmental damage. Iran and neighboring Gulf states have limited environmental cooperation due to political tensions. Climate change threatens Gulf marine ecosystems.
laws.penalty: Fines for marine pollution; criminal penalties for deliberate oil spills
exceptions: Military vessels have some exemptions from civilian environmental rules
Emergency response provisions for oil spills
laws.source: Iranian Environmental Protection Organization; Gulf Marine Environment Data

quiz.q: How long is Iran's coastline along the Persian Gulf?
quiz.explanation: Iran has over 1,700 km of coastline along the Persian Gulf, making Iranian offshore oil operations and coastal industrial activities significant contributors to environmental threats in this heavily polluted body of water.

laws.title: Freedom of Assembly and Protest
laws.subtitle: Constitutional right with extensive practical restrictions
laws.fullDescription: Iran's constitution nominally guarantees the right to peaceful assembly. In practice, any gathering critical of the government is suppressed with lethal force. The 2022 Woman, Life, Freedom protests saw security forces use live ammunition, birdshot, metal pellets, and other lethal force against protesters. Iran's security forces — IRGC, Basij, and police — have used crowd control weapons causing mass blinding of protesters. The Supreme National Security Council can prohibit any assembly.
laws.penalty: Criminal prosecution of protest organizers; violence against participants
exceptions: State-sanctioned rallies (e.g., pro-government demonstrations) are freely permitted
Religious processions and Friday prayers are permitted
laws.source: Iranian Constitution, Article 27; Protest suppression documentation

quiz.q: What weapon used against 2022 protesters caused mass blinding injuries in Iran?
options: Birdshot and metal pellets fired at faces
quiz.explanation: Security forces firing birdshot and metal pellets directly at protesters' faces caused mass blinding injuries during Iran's 2022 protests, with hundreds of people reportedly losing partial or full eyesight as a result.

laws.title: Tehran Stock Exchange
laws.subtitle: Capital markets under sanctions pressure
laws.fullDescription: The Tehran Stock Exchange (TSE) is one of the Middle East's larger stock exchanges, with hundreds of listed companies. Iran's equity market has experienced extreme volatility due to sanctions, currency devaluation, and political uncertainty. Many Iranians invested in the stock market as a hedge against inflation, leading to a stock market bubble in 2020 that subsequently crashed, wiping out savings for millions of retail investors. Foreign investors are largely excluded from the TSE due to sanctions.
laws.penalty: Criminal penalties for market manipulation and securities fraud
exceptions: Some foreign nationals from non-sanctioning countries can invest
IRGC-affiliated companies operate with less regulatory scrutiny
laws.source: Securities and Exchange Organization of Iran; Tehran Stock Exchange

quiz.q: What happened to Iran's stock market in 2020 that wiped out savings for millions of retail investors?
options: A government-induced crash to punish speculators
A bubble formed as Iranians hedged against inflation, then crashed
quiz.explanation: Iran's 2020 stock market saw a bubble form as ordinary Iranians invested to hedge against inflation and currency devaluation, encouraged by government promotion. The subsequent crash wiped out savings for millions of retail investors.

laws.title: Territorial Disputes — Three UAE Islands
laws.subtitle: Occupation of Abu Musa and Greater and Lesser Tunbs
laws.fullDescription: Iran occupies three islands — Abu Musa and the Greater and Lesser Tunbs — that the UAE claims. Iran seized the islands in 1971 at the time of British withdrawal from the Gulf. The UAE and Arab League demand their return. Iranian law treats the islands as sovereign Iranian territory, and any challenge to this is considered sedition. The dispute affects Iran-UAE and broader Iran-Arab world relations. Iran uses the islands' strategic location to monitor Gulf shipping.
laws.penalty: Treason charges for any Iranian official challenging sovereignty over the three islands
exceptions: Diplomatic negotiations on the matter are not officially occurring
Islands treated as fully integrated Iranian territory
laws.source: Iranian Constitutional Territory; UN General Assembly Resolutions on the Islands

quiz.q: When did Iran seize the three islands of Abu Musa and the Greater and Lesser Tunbs?
quiz.explanation: Iran seized the three islands of Abu Musa, Greater Tunb, and Lesser Tunb in 1971 at the time of Britain's withdrawal from the Persian Gulf, and has occupied them since despite UAE claims to sovereignty.

laws.title: Persian Language — Official Language Policy
laws.subtitle: Persian as the sole official language
laws.fullDescription: The Iranian constitution designates Persian (Farsi) as the official and instructional language. While the constitution permits minority language use in the press and schools alongside Persian, in practice minority language education is limited. Iran's Azeri Turkish, Kurdish, Arabic, Balochi, and Turkmen speakers face restrictions on native language education. The Arabic script used for Persian is mandated. Cultural identity is closely tied to the Persian language, creating tensions with minority communities.
laws.penalty: N/A — language policy; minority language activists face national security charges
exceptions: Religious instruction in recognized minority languages permitted
Private cultural associations can operate in minority languages with restrictions
laws.source: Iranian Constitution, Articles 15-16

quiz.q: What does Iran's constitution permit for minority languages despite Persian being official?
options: No minority language use in any public setting
Minority language use in the press and schools alongside Persian (though limited in practice)
Full bilingual education in all minority regions
Minority languages as co-official in their regions
quiz.explanation: Iran's constitution permits minority language use in the press and schools alongside Persian, but in practice minority language education is severely limited, creating tensions with Azeri, Kurdish, Arab, Baloch, and Turkmen communities.

laws.title: Iran's Export of Revolution
laws.subtitle: Constitutional mandate to support revolutionary movements
laws.fullDescription: Article 154 of Iran's constitution explicitly states that Iran supports 'the just struggle of the oppressed against the oppressors in any part of the world.' This provides constitutional justification for the IRGC's proxy activities across the Middle East. The principle of 'exporting the revolution' has underpinned Iranian foreign policy since 1979. Critics argue this has fueled regional instability. Supporters say it reflects Iran's anti-imperialist foreign policy. This constitutional mandate creates direct tension with international law.
laws.penalty: N/A — constitutional foreign policy principle
exceptions: Diplomatic engagement coexists with revolutionary export doctrine
Pragmatic interests sometimes override revolutionary ideology
laws.source: Iranian Constitution, Article 154

quiz.q: What does Article 154 of Iran's constitution state about revolutionary movements?
options: Iran remains neutral in all foreign conflicts
Iran only supports Persian-speaking populations abroad
Iran supports the just struggle of the oppressed against the oppressors worldwide
Iran supports only Islamic revolutionary movements
quiz.explanation: Article 154 of Iran's constitution explicitly states that Iran supports 'the just struggle of the oppressed against the oppressors in any part of the world,' providing a constitutional mandate for Iran's support of proxy forces and regional interventions.

laws.title: Lawyers — Disbarment and Prosecution
laws.subtitle: Human rights lawyers prosecuted for defending clients
laws.fullDescription: Iranian human rights lawyers face systematic prosecution for doing their jobs. The Islamic Lawyers Association has been shut down. Prominent human rights lawyers including Nobel laureate Shirin Ebadi (now in exile) and Nasrin Sotoudeh (repeatedly imprisoned) have been disbarred and imprisoned for representing political defendants, women's rights activists, and journalists. Lawyers representing protesters from the 2022 uprising were themselves arrested. The state effectively controls the legal profession.
laws.penalty: Imprisonment and disbarment for lawyers deemed to have undermined national security
exceptions: Lawyers representing defendants in approved cases operate without restriction
State-assigned defense lawyers operate within approved parameters
laws.source: Iranian Bar Association; Human Rights Watch documentation of lawyer prosecutions

quiz.q: Which Iranian human rights lawyer received the Nobel Peace Prize in 2003?
quiz.explanation: Shirin Ebadi received the Nobel Peace Prize in 2003 for her work on human rights and democracy in Iran, becoming the first Iranian and first Muslim woman to receive the prize. She has been living in exile since 2009.

laws.title: Urban Development — Tehran Megacity
laws.subtitle: Rapid urbanization and infrastructure challenges
laws.fullDescription: Tehran, Iran's capital, is a megacity of over 15 million people in the greater metropolitan area. Rapid urbanization has strained infrastructure, housing, and environmental quality. The Tehran master plan attempts to guide urban development. Earthquake risk is a major concern — Tehran sits above multiple fault lines and a major earthquake could be catastrophic. Building regulations require earthquake-resistant construction, but enforcement of older buildings is limited. Urban sprawl has consumed agricultural land.
laws.penalty: Fines for building code violations; criminal charges for construction fraud causing deaths
exceptions: Historic buildings have special preservation rules
Informal settlements in outer areas tolerated but not legalized
laws.source: Tehran Metropolitan Area Plans; Building Regulations

quiz.q: What major natural hazard poses a catastrophic risk to Tehran?
options: Major earthquake — Tehran sits above multiple fault lines
quiz.explanation: Tehran sits above multiple fault lines and faces catastrophic earthquake risk — a major earthquake under Tehran's dense urban area could result in massive casualties and infrastructure destruction, making earthquake preparedness a critical policy issue.

laws.title: Shia Islam — State Religion
laws.subtitle: Islamic law as constitutional foundation
laws.fullDescription: Iran's constitution establishes Shia (Twelver Ja'fari) Islam as the state religion, with all laws required to conform to Islamic jurisprudence. The Guardian Council reviews all legislation for conformity with Islam. Sunni Muslims (approximately 5-10% of Iran's population, including many Kurds, Baloch, and Turkmen) face discrimination in government employment and the construction of Sunni mosques in Tehran. The Shia character of the state affects all aspects of law and governance.
laws.penalty: N/A — religious establishment provision
exceptions: Recognized non-Muslim minorities (Christian, Jewish, Zoroastrian) have protected status
Sunni Muslims can practice privately but face employment discrimination
laws.source: Iranian Constitution, Article 12

quiz.q: What sect of Islam is established as Iran's state religion?
quiz.explanation: Iran's constitution establishes Twelver Ja'fari (Shia) Islam as the official state religion, requiring all laws to conform to Islamic jurisprudence as interpreted by Shia scholars, and giving Iran's clerical establishment constitutional authority.

laws.title: Wrongful Detention — International Cases
laws.subtitle: Pattern of detaining foreigners for diplomatic leverage
laws.fullDescription: The UN Working Group on Arbitrary Detention has repeatedly found Iran's detention of foreigners and dual nationals to constitute arbitrary detention under international law. Notable cases include Jason Rezaian (Washington Post journalist, released 2016 in prisoner exchange), Nazanin Zaghari-Ratcliffe (British-Iranian, imprisoned 2016-2022), and the Emami brothers. Iran has used prisoner exchanges to obtain concessions including frozen funds and the release of Iranian nationals held abroad. The pattern constitutes a systematic policy rather than individual cases.
laws.penalty: Extensive imprisonment under national security charges
exceptions: Prisoner exchanges have resolved many high-profile cases
Some detainees released on humanitarian grounds with international pressure
laws.source: UN Working Group on Arbitrary Detention; Individual case documentation
laws.sourceLabel: Iran Arbitrary Detention of Foreign Nationals

quiz.q: How long was British-Iranian Nazanin Zaghari-Ratcliffe imprisoned in Iran?
quiz.explanation: Nazanin Zaghari-Ratcliffe was imprisoned in Iran from 2016 to 2022 — approximately 6 years — before her release following extensive diplomatic negotiations and a British payment of a disputed debt to Iran.

laws.title: Corruption — Systemic Problem
laws.subtitle: Widespread corruption in state and economy
