laws.fullDescription: Iran scores poorly on international corruption indices (Transparency International CPI). Corruption is embedded in the system through the opaque bonyad system, IRGC economic activities, nepotism in government employment, and bribery in the bureaucracy. High-profile corruption cases have been prosecuted selectively as political tools rather than systematic enforcement. The 2018-2019 period saw several executions of individuals convicted of financial corruption — some of whom may have been political targets.
laws.penalty: Imprisonment up to 25 years and execution for grand corruption
exceptions: IRGC-linked entities and bonyads largely immune from corruption investigations
Political connections provide significant protection
laws.source: Transparency International CPI; Iranian Anti-Corruption Law

quiz.q: How has Iran used high-profile corruption prosecutions according to critics?
options: As a genuine anti-corruption enforcement mechanism
As selective political tools rather than systematic enforcement
To comply with UN Convention Against Corruption
quiz.explanation: Critics note that Iran's high-profile corruption prosecutions are used selectively as political tools — to target rivals or make examples — rather than representing systematic anti-corruption enforcement, with IRGC-linked entities largely immune.

laws.title: Velayat-e Faqih in Daily Life
laws.subtitle: Supreme Leader's authority affects all aspects of law
laws.fullDescription: The doctrine of Velayat-e Faqih (Guardianship of the Islamic Jurist) means the Supreme Leader's authority extends to all areas of Iranian law and daily life. The Supreme Leader issues religious decrees (fatwa) that have the force of law. His approval is needed for major policies. He controls the military, judiciary, state media, and can dissolve parliament in extreme cases. The current Supreme Leader, Ali Khamenei, has held the position since 1989. There is no democratic accountability for this position.
laws.penalty: Insulting the Supreme Leader is a criminal offense (5-10 years imprisonment)
exceptions: Theological debate within approved frameworks is permitted
Some matters left to elected officials within the Leader's overall framework
laws.source: Iranian Constitution, Articles 5, 57, 107-112

quiz.q: Since what year has Ali Khamenei been Iran's Supreme Leader?
quiz.explanation: Ali Khamenei became Iran's Supreme Leader in 1989 following the death of Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini. As Supreme Leader, Khamenei has held supreme authority over all branches of government for over three decades.

laws.title: Blood Money (Diya) — Discriminatory Values
laws.subtitle: Different compensation amounts based on religion and gender
laws.fullDescription: Iran's Diya (blood money) system assigns different monetary values to human life based on religion and gender. A Muslim man's Diya is the highest; a Muslim woman's is half a man's; a non-Muslim's Diya (for Christians, Jews, Zoroastrians) is historically lower. The Diya for a Bahá'í is not legally recognized. The Diya amount (set annually based on gold prices) is paid by a perpetrator to a victim's family as compensation in lieu of Qisas punishment. Foreign nationals face difficulties claiming Diya abroad.
laws.penalty: Diya payments are civil compensation in criminal cases; failure to pay allows Qisas to proceed
exceptions: 2012 amendment equalized Diya between Muslim and non-Muslim recognized minorities in some cases
Foreign nationals' Diya determined by reciprocity principles
laws.source: Iranian Islamic Penal Code, 2013, Book Four (Diya)

quiz.q: How does a Muslim woman's Diya (blood money) compare to a Muslim man's under Iranian law?
quiz.explanation: Under Iran's Diya system, a Muslim woman's blood money is set at half the value of a Muslim man's — a provision codifying gender inequality that has been widely criticized by international human rights bodies.

laws.title: Territorial Integrity — Ethnic Minority Regions
laws.subtitle: Constitutional provisions on territorial unity
laws.fullDescription: Iran's constitution declares the indivisibility of the Iranian homeland and prohibits any action that would challenge territorial integrity. This provision is used to justify suppressing autonomy movements among Kurdish, Arab, Baloch, and Azerbaijani minorities. The Kurdish PJAK (Party of Free Life of Kurdistan) and Arab separatist groups in Khuzestan have been designated terrorist organizations. Military operations, summary executions, and collective punishment have been used in minority regions.
laws.penalty: Death penalty for separatist activities; long imprisonment for autonomy advocacy
exceptions: Cultural expression within approved frameworks is permitted
Local governance within the centralized state structure is permitted
laws.source: Iranian Constitution, Articles 1 and 9

quiz.q: What constitutional principle justifies Iran's suppression of ethnic autonomy movements?
options: Constitutional indivisibility of the Iranian homeland
quiz.explanation: Iran's constitution declares the indivisibility of the Iranian homeland, providing the constitutional justification for suppressing Kurdish, Arab, Baloch, and Azerbaijani autonomy movements as threats to territorial integrity.

laws.title: Drug Policy — Addiction Treatment
laws.subtitle: Harm reduction alongside criminal enforcement
laws.fullDescription: Iran has a large drug addiction problem — an estimated 2-3 million drug users. The Iranian government has implemented progressive harm reduction policies including needle exchange programs and methadone maintenance treatment, reducing HIV transmission among drug users. This pragmatic public health approach coexists with severe criminal penalties for trafficking. Iran faces a major challenge from proximity to Afghanistan, which produces 80%+ of the world's opium. Treatment centers are publicly funded.
laws.penalty: Treatment programs for addicts; criminal prosecution for trafficking
exceptions: Drug users who register for treatment may avoid prosecution
Needle exchange and harm reduction programs operate legally
laws.source: Iranian State Welfare Organization; Anti-Narcotics Law

quiz.q: What harm reduction policies has Iran implemented despite its harsh drug trafficking laws?
options: Needle exchange programs and methadone maintenance treatment
quiz.explanation: Despite severe criminal penalties for drug trafficking, Iran has implemented progressive harm reduction policies including needle exchange programs and methadone maintenance treatment, which have successfully reduced HIV transmission among drug users.

laws.title: Persian Cultural Heritage
laws.subtitle: Legal protection of Iran's ancient cultural heritage
laws.fullDescription: Iran is home to extraordinary cultural heritage including Persepolis (UNESCO World Heritage), Pasargadae, Isfahan's historic district, Yazd, and numerous other sites. The Iranian Cultural Heritage Organization (now Ministry of Cultural Heritage) protects these sites. Unauthorized excavation and export of antiquities is criminalized. Iran has sought repatriation of artifacts held in foreign museums. Concerns about the 2020 US threat to target cultural sites during tensions were widely condemned internationally.
laws.penalty: Imprisonment up to 10 years and heavy fines for looting or damaging heritage sites
exceptions: Authorized archaeological excavations by international teams historically permitted
Emergency preservation work may proceed without standard permissions
laws.source: Iranian Law on the Protection of Historical Heritage

quiz.q: Which ancient Persian site is an UNESCO World Heritage Site that was the ceremonial capital of the Achaemenid Empire?
quiz.explanation: Persepolis (Takht-e Jamshid) is an UNESCO World Heritage Site that served as the ceremonial capital of the Achaemenid Persian Empire, built by Darius I around 518 BCE and now one of Iran's most iconic historical monuments.

laws.title: Social Media Arrests
laws.subtitle: Prosecution for online speech and activism
laws.fullDescription: Iran has significantly increased arrests for social media activity, particularly since the 2022 protests. Instagram posts, Telegram messages, tweets, and WhatsApp messages have been used as evidence in criminal prosecutions. The Cybercrime Police (FATA) monitors social media and coordinates arrests. Mourners posting tributes to protesters killed by security forces have been arrested. Journalists posting from inside Iran face particularly severe risks. Self-censorship has become widespread.
laws.penalty: Imprisonment 1-10 years for social media posts deemed against national security or insulting the Supreme Leader
exceptions: Pro-government content freely permitted
Approved commentary within official media frameworks
laws.source: Iranian Cybercrime Law; FATA (Cybercrime Police) activities

quiz.q: What Iranian police unit is responsible for monitoring social media and coordinating arrests?
quiz.explanation: FATA (the Iranian Cybercrime Police) is the specialized unit that monitors social media platforms, coordinates arrests of users for online speech, and enforces Iran's Cybercrime Law against digital dissent.

laws.title: Teacher and Worker Protests
laws.subtitle: Labor activism met with arrest
laws.fullDescription: Iran's teachers and workers have organized independent protests demanding wage increases, release of imprisoned colleagues, and better conditions. The Iranian Teachers' Trade Association and workers' councils that operate outside the state-approved Islamic Labour Council framework face systematic suppression. Labor activists including Reza Shahabi (bus workers' union) and Esmaeil Bakhshi (Haft Tappeh sugar cane workers) have been repeatedly arrested and tortured in detention. Worker protests have increased amid economic deterioration from sanctions.
laws.penalty: Criminal charges including 'propaganda against the state' and 'gathering against national security'
exceptions: State-approved Islamic Labour Councils can raise issues within the system
Petition processes to Ministry of Labour available
laws.source: Iran Labour News Agency; Human Rights Watch labor documentation

quiz.q: What happened to Iranian labor activist Esmaeil Bakhshi of the Haft Tappeh sugar cane workers?
options: He was promoted to government mediator
He received the ILO Decent Work Prize
He was repeatedly arrested and reportedly tortured in detention
He led a successful strike that resulted in wage increases
quiz.explanation: Esmaeil Bakhshi, a leader of the Haft Tappeh sugar cane workers' independent union, was repeatedly arrested and reportedly tortured in detention after organizing strikes for unpaid wages, becoming a symbol of labor repression in Iran.

laws.title: IRGC — Constitutional Status
laws.subtitle: Revolutionary Guards as a constitutional institution
laws.fullDescription: The Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC) is enshrined in Iran's constitution as a force to protect the revolution alongside the regular military. The IRGC answers to the Supreme Leader rather than the President or parliament. The IRGC has grown from a revolutionary militia into a powerful military, economic, and political institution. It commands the nuclear and ballistic missile programs. The IRGC's constitutional status insulates it from democratic accountability.
laws.penalty: Insulting or undermining the IRGC is treated as a national security offense
exceptions: Regular military (Artesh) operates parallel to IRGC with more conventional role
President can appoint Defense Minister but IRGC commanders appointed by Supreme Leader
laws.source: Iranian Constitution, Article 150

quiz.q: To whom does Iran's IRGC primarily answer, rather than to elected officials?
quiz.explanation: Iran's IRGC is constitutionally established and answers primarily to the Supreme Leader rather than to the elected President or parliament, giving the Supreme Leader direct control over this powerful military, economic, and political institution.

laws.title: Climate Change Vulnerability
laws.subtitle: Iran faces severe climate change impacts
laws.fullDescription: Iran is highly vulnerable to climate change impacts including prolonged drought, desertification, dust storms, extreme heat events, and floods. The Lake Urmia crisis and Khuzestan water shortages are partly climate-related. Climate change has exacerbated internal displacement from rural to urban areas. International sanctions have limited Iran's ability to access clean energy technology and international climate finance. Iran submitted NDCs under the Paris Agreement but compliance is hampered by economic conditions.
laws.penalty: N/A — climate policy framework
exceptions: International climate finance theoretically available but sanctions complicate access
Renewable energy development permitted within domestic regulatory framework
laws.source: Iranian NDC; IPCC Reports on Middle East/North Africa

quiz.q: What climate crisis in Khuzestan province led to protests in 2021?
options: Severe heat waves causing mass illness
Water shortages and drying of the Karun and Dez rivers
quiz.explanation: Protests in Iran's Khuzestan province in 2021 were sparked by severe water shortages, including the drying of rivers like the Karun and Dez due to a combination of dam construction, agricultural overuse, and climate-exacerbated drought.

laws.title: Iran Nuclear Deal — Legal Framework
laws.subtitle: JCPOA and its domestic legal implications
laws.fullDescription: The Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action (JCPOA), signed in 2015, was a landmark agreement between Iran and the P5+1 (US, UK, France, Germany, Russia, China) limiting Iran's nuclear program in exchange for sanctions relief. Iran's parliament passed the Law on Implementing the JCPOA, but after the US withdrew in 2018 under President Trump, Iran progressively reduced compliance. The 2021 Vienna talks sought to restore the JCPOA but remained unresolved. Iran's nuclear enrichment has significantly increased above JCPOA limits.
laws.penalty: N/A — international agreement; domestic law implements Iran's obligations
exceptions: Supreme Leader retains authority to override any nuclear deal commitments
Domestic law on nuclear development cannot be changed by executive alone
laws.source: JCPOA 2015; Law on Implementing the JCPOA; IAEA Reports

quiz.q: Which countries were involved in negotiating the JCPOA nuclear deal with Iran?
options: P5+1: US, UK, France, Germany, Russia, and China
quiz.explanation: The JCPOA (Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action) was negotiated between Iran and the P5+1: the five permanent members of the UN Security Council (US, UK, France, Russia, China) plus Germany, representing a major multilateral diplomatic achievement.

laws.title: Anti-LGBTQ+ Enforcement
laws.subtitle: Policing and punishment of LGBTQ+ persons
laws.fullDescription: Iran's security forces actively police LGBTQ+ persons. Police raids on private parties, entrapping gay men online, and monitoring social media have led to arrests. LGBTQ+ Iranians face violence, forced psychiatric treatment, and family pressure to conform. Many have sought asylum in Turkey and other countries before applying for resettlement in Western countries. The Islamic Republic has executed individuals for homosexuality since 1979 — estimates range from hundreds to thousands of executions.
laws.penalty: Flogging, imprisonment, or death penalty depending on acts and evidence
exceptions: Transgender persons who conform to assigned gender after surgery may avoid prosecution
Private consensual acts difficult to prove without confession or witnesses
laws.source: Iranian Islamic Penal Code; ILGA World Reports

quiz.q: What has happened to LGBTQ+ Iranians seeking safety from persecution?
options: They have been given protected status within Iran
Many have sought asylum in Turkey before applying for Western resettlement
They have found protection in recognized minority religious communities
Iran has established safe zones for LGBTQ+ persons
quiz.explanation: Many LGBTQ+ Iranians have fled persecution by seeking asylum in Turkey (which allows visa-free entry for Iranians) before applying for resettlement in Western countries through UNHCR, as internal flight alternatives within Iran are unavailable.

laws.title: Sanctions Evasion Networks
laws.subtitle: Iran's methods to circumvent international sanctions
laws.fullDescription: Iran has developed sophisticated methods to circumvent international sanctions including: using shell companies in third countries, selling oil through shadow tanker networks, cryptocurrency transactions, front companies in Turkey, UAE, and China, and barter arrangements. The US Treasury's OFAC regularly designates new entities involved in sanctions evasion. Iran's ability to continue oil exports through these mechanisms has partially offset the sanctions impact. Chinese companies have been major purchasers of sanctioned Iranian oil.
laws.penalty: US and international penalties for entities assisting sanctions evasion; Iranian law rewards such evasion
exceptions: Humanitarian trade has partial exemptions in principle
Certain Chinese entities accept consequences in exchange for discounted oil
laws.source: US OFAC Designations; Iranian Central Bank reports

quiz.q: What type of transactions has Iran used to evade traditional banking sanctions?
options: Cryptocurrency transactions, shadow tanker networks, and shell companies
quiz.explanation: Iran has developed multiple sanctions evasion methods including cryptocurrency transactions, shadow tanker networks for oil exports, shell companies in third countries, and barter arrangements — sophisticated techniques documented by US OFAC.

laws.title: Academic Freedom — Politically Sensitive Research
laws.subtitle: Restrictions on research and publication
laws.fullDescription: Iranian academics face significant restrictions on research topics deemed politically or religiously sensitive. Topics related to ethnic minority history, political dissent, comparative religion, gender studies beyond approved frameworks, and certain historical periods are constrained. Academics have been dismissed and imprisoned for research and publications. Iranian universities have brain drain problems as academics seek positions abroad. Social science and humanities are more restricted than STEM disciplines. International academic collaborations are constrained by sanctions.
laws.penalty: Dismissal from university positions; criminal charges for published material
exceptions: Hard sciences have more academic freedom
Approved political science within the revolutionary framework is taught
laws.source: Iranian Higher Education Council; Academic Freedom Monitor

quiz.q: Which academic disciplines face more restrictions in Iran compared to others?
options: Social sciences and humanities compared to STEM
quiz.explanation: Social sciences and humanities face significantly more restrictions in Iran compared to STEM fields, as topics in history, political science, sociology, and gender studies are more likely to touch on politically and religiously sensitive areas.

laws.title: Environmental Activists — Persecution
laws.subtitle: Arrest and prosecution of environmental defenders
laws.fullDescription: Iranian environmental activists and researchers have faced severe persecution. The 2018 arrest of eight wildlife conservationists (Persian Cheetah researchers, including Iranian-American Kavous Seyed-Emami who died in custody) on espionage charges shocked the international scientific community. The arrests sent a chilling message to all environmental work in Iran. Multiple environmentalists remain imprisoned. Iran faces environmental crises (water, dust storms, biodiversity loss) that require scientific expertise the government is persecuting.
laws.penalty: Espionage charges carrying up to death penalty; imprisonment for 'contact with foreigners'
exceptions: State-approved environmental work through official channels permitted
Traditional conservation tied to hunting management has some space
laws.source: Persian Wildlife Heritage Foundation; Human Rights Watch

quiz.q: What happened to Iranian-American environmentalist Kavous Seyed-Emami after his 2018 arrest on espionage charges?
options: He was deported to the United States
He was sentenced to life imprisonment
quiz.explanation: Kavous Seyed-Emami, an Iranian-American wildlife conservationist working on Persian Cheetah conservation, died in custody in 2018 shortly after his arrest on espionage charges, with authorities claiming suicide but his family and human rights groups questioning this account.

laws.title: Judiciary — Clerical Control
laws.subtitle: Judicial system under clerical authority
laws.fullDescription: Iran's judiciary is constitutionally required to be headed by a mojtahed (qualified Shia jurist) appointed by the Supreme Leader. The judiciary thus operates as an arm of clerical power rather than an independent branch of government. The head of the judiciary appoints the chief of the Supreme Court and Prosecutor General. Judges are selected for their ideological commitment alongside legal training. Women cannot serve as full judges in Iran's court system (though there have been incremental changes). This constitutional design prevents genuine judicial independence.
laws.penalty: N/A — judicial structure
exceptions: Lower court judges include legally-trained women in advisory roles in some courts
Administrative courts have somewhat less clerical orientation
laws.source: Iranian Constitution, Articles 156-162

quiz.q: What qualification must the Head of Iran's Judiciary hold?
options: Law degree from a recognized university
At least 20 years of legal experience
Mojtahed — a qualified Shia Islamic jurist
quiz.explanation: Iran's constitution requires the Head of the Judiciary to be a mojtahed — a qualified Shia Islamic jurist — appointed by the Supreme Leader, ensuring the judiciary operates as an arm of clerical power rather than an independent branch of government.

laws.title: Executions of 2022 Protest Leaders
laws.subtitle: Death sentences and executions following Woman, Life, Freedom protests
laws.fullDescription: Following the 2022 Woman, Life, Freedom protests, Iranian courts sentenced dozens of protesters to death and carried out at least 9 executions by early 2024. Those executed were convicted of moharebeh (enmity against God) and 'spreading corruption on earth.' International outcry including protests in Europe, North America, and around the world failed to prevent the executions. Multiple UN special rapporteurs condemned the trials as failing minimum fair trial standards.
laws.penalty: Execution carried out; many others on death row pending appeals
exceptions: International pressure delayed some executions temporarily
Some convictions reduced on appeal from death to imprisonment
laws.source: Iran Human Rights organization; UN Special Rapporteur Reports 2022-2023

quiz.q: On what charges were protesters executed following Iran's 2022 demonstrations?
options: Moharebeh (enmity against God) and spreading corruption on earth
quiz.explanation: Protesters executed after Iran's 2022 demonstrations were convicted of moharebeh (enmity against God) and 'spreading corruption on earth' — broad charges used against political opponents that carry the death penalty under Iran's Islamic Penal Code.

laws.title: Women in the Workforce
laws.subtitle: Legal and cultural barriers to women's employment
laws.fullDescription: Iranian women face significant legal and cultural barriers in the workforce. Women must have their husband's permission to work in many occupations. Women cannot work in certain jobs, travel without spousal permission, or obtain a passport without approval. Despite these restrictions, women have high educational attainment (majority of university graduates are women) and significant presence in medicine, academia, and some professions. Many women have circumvented restrictions through creative legal strategies.
laws.penalty: Restrictions built into civil and administrative law rather than criminal penalties
exceptions: Single women and widows have fewer restrictions
Professional women in medicine and academia have significant practical autonomy
Divorce or separation can free women from spouse permission requirements
laws.source: Iranian Civil Code; Labour Law gender provisions

quiz.q: What educational trend in Iran contradicts the legal and cultural barriers women face?
options: Women have lower literacy rates than men
Women are majority of university graduates despite employment restrictions
Women dominate STEM fields but not humanities
Women attend university at the same rate as men
quiz.explanation: Despite significant legal and cultural employment barriers, Iranian women represent the majority of university graduates — a striking paradox where high educational attainment has not translated proportionally into labor market participation or legal equality.

laws.title: Book Censorship
laws.subtitle: Ministry of Culture approves all publications
laws.fullDescription: Iran's Ministry of Culture and Islamic Guidance must approve all books before publication. The approval process can take months or years, and many books are simply rejected. Books by opposition figures, books on sexuality, books critical of Islam or the government, and books deemed un-Islamic are banned. Western novels must be reviewed and may have passages removed. Many Iranian authors have been imprisoned and their books banned. A thriving underground book scene exists despite censorship.
laws.penalty: Criminal penalties for publishing without approval; imprisonment for authors of banned books
exceptions: Academic publications may have slightly more latitude
Books already in circulation before 1979 may remain on shelves
laws.source: Iranian Press Law; Ministry of Culture and Islamic Guidance regulations

quiz.q: What process must all books in Iran go through before publication?
options: Review and approval by the Ministry of Culture and Islamic Guidance
quiz.explanation: All books in Iran must receive approval from the Ministry of Culture and Islamic Guidance (Ershad) before publication — a censorship process that can take months and results in many books being permanently rejected or requiring revisions.

laws.title: Persian Cheetah Conservation
laws.subtitle: Protection of the world's rarest big cat
laws.fullDescription: The Asiatic Cheetah (Acinonyx jubatus venaticus) is critically endangered with fewer than 20 individuals surviving exclusively in Iran. Iran hosts the last surviving population of this subspecies. The Iranian government has conservation programs for the Persian cheetah, and killing a cheetah is a serious criminal offense. However, the 2018 arrest of conservationists on espionage charges severely damaged conservation efforts. Climate change, road kills, and prey depletion threaten the remaining population.
laws.penalty: Imprisonment up to 10 years and heavy fines for killing a protected cheetah
exceptions: Scientific research with permits
Captive breeding program animals handled by authorized personnel
laws.source: Iranian Department of Environment; IUCN Asiatic Cheetah assessment

quiz.q: How many Asiatic Cheetahs are estimated to survive, all in Iran?
quiz.explanation: The Asiatic Cheetah is critically endangered with fewer than 20 individuals surviving, all in Iran, making it the world's rarest big cat. Iran hosts the entire world population of this subspecies.

laws.title: Iran 1979 Revolution — Constitutional Legacy
laws.subtitle: The revolutionary constitution and its 45-year impact
laws.fullDescription: The Islamic Revolution of 1979 overthrew the Pahlavi monarchy and established the Islamic Republic under Ayatollah Khomeini. The 1979 constitution (revised 1989) encoded the principle of Velayat-e Faqih as the supreme governing principle. Forty-five years later, the constitutional structures established in 1979 remain fundamentally unchanged despite significant evolution in Iranian society. The revolutionary generation is aging while younger Iranians (the majority having been born after the revolution) increasingly challenge the system, as shown by the 2022 protests.
laws.penalty: N/A — historical/constitutional context
exceptions: Constitutional reform requires Supreme Leader approval
Incremental changes have occurred within the fundamental revolutionary framework
laws.source: Iranian Constitution 1979 (revised 1989); Revolutionary history

quiz.q: In what year was Iran's revolutionary constitution revised to incorporate the Supreme Leader's expanded powers?
quiz.explanation: Iran's constitution was significantly revised in 1989 following Ayatollah Khomeini's death, with the revision expanding the Supreme Leader's powers and creating the Expediency Council, cementing the constitutional framework that governs Iran today.

laws.title: Confiscated Property — Post-Revolution
laws.subtitle: Properties seized after 1979 revolution
laws.fullDescription: After the 1979 revolution, the Islamic Republic confiscated vast amounts of property from the Pahlavi family, foreign companies, and individuals who fled or were deemed enemies of the revolution. The Foundation of the Oppressed (Bonyad Mostazafin) was established to manage confiscated assets. Jewish community properties, Bahá'í assets, and properties belonging to those executed or exiled were seized. Many families have never received compensation or restitution. Descendants abroad continue to seek return of their properties through international legal mechanisms.
laws.penalty: N/A — historical confiscation policy
exceptions: Iranian courts nominally allow property claims but rarely rule against the state
Diplomatic negotiations have resolved some foreign company claims
laws.source: Islamic Republic of Iran Confiscation Decrees 1979-1983

quiz.q: What foundation was established to manage properties confiscated after the 1979 revolution?
quiz.explanation: The Foundation of the Oppressed (Bonyad Mostazafin) was established after the 1979 revolution to manage confiscated properties, and has grown into one of Iran's largest economic conglomerates controlling factories, hotels, farms, and other assets.

laws.title: Anti-Corruption — Selective Enforcement
laws.subtitle: Anti-corruption prosecutions as political tools
laws.fullDescription: Iran has prosecuted many individuals for financial corruption, but enforcement is widely seen as selective — targeting political rivals or making examples while IRGC-linked entities and bonyads remain largely immune. In 2019, Akbar Tabari, a senior judiciary official, was sentenced to 31 years for corruption. Several businesspeople connected to the reformist camp have been prosecuted. The 2018-2019 executions of businessmen for corruption were criticized as politically motivated.
laws.penalty: Imprisonment up to life; execution for 'corruption on earth' in economic cases
exceptions: IRGC economic activities rarely investigated
Supreme Leader-adjacent businesses protected from scrutiny
laws.source: Iranian Anti-Corruption Law; High-profile corruption case records

quiz.q: How are Iran's anti-corruption prosecutions criticized?
options: Selective — targeting political rivals while IRGC and bonyads remain largely immune
quiz.explanation: Iran's anti-corruption prosecutions are widely criticized as selective political tools — targeting political rivals and reformists while IRGC-linked entities and religious foundations (bonyads) remain largely immune from investigation.

laws.title: Internet Governance — National Intranet
laws.subtitle: Building a domestic internet to replace the global web
laws.fullDescription: Iran has been developing its National Information Network (NIN) — a domestic intranet — since 2011, aiming to create an alternative to the global internet that remains under state control even during complete international internet cutoffs. During the 2019 protests, Iran shut down the global internet for almost a week while the national network remained operational for government communications. The NIN hosts government services, domestic email, and approved content. This 'sovereign internet' model influences similar projects in Russia and China.
laws.penalty: Criminal penalties for circumventing national network controls
exceptions: Government agencies operate on secure networks regardless of internet status
Approved businesses receive special connectivity
laws.source: Iranian National Information Network Policy; Cybercrime Law

quiz.q: For how long did Iran shut down the global internet during 2019 protests?
quiz.explanation: During Iran's 2019 protests against fuel price increases, the government shut down access to the global internet for almost a week while maintaining the domestic National Information Network, representing one of the most extensive internet shutdowns ever recorded.

laws.title: Majlis — Iran's Parliament
laws.subtitle: Elected parliament within constrained system
laws.fullDescription: Iran's Majlis (Islamic Consultative Assembly) has 290 members elected every 4 years. All legislation must comply with Islamic law and be approved by the Guardian Council, which reviews all bills for Islamic conformity. The Majlis can question and impeach the President and ministers. Despite its constrained role, the Majlis has been a site of genuine political debate within the revolutionary system. Guardian Council vetting means only approved candidates can run, limiting genuine representation.
laws.penalty: N/A — legislative body
exceptions: Majlis can override some Guardian Council objections via Expediency Council
Some independent voices occasionally win seats in approved elections
laws.source: Iranian Constitution, Articles 62-90

quiz.q: How many members does Iran's Majlis (parliament) have?
quiz.explanation: Iran's Majlis (Islamic Consultative Assembly) has 290 members elected every 4 years, though all legislation is subject to Guardian Council review for Islamic conformity, significantly limiting the parliament's effective legislative independence.

laws.title: Satellite Dishes — Illegal But Tolerated
laws.subtitle: De facto tolerance of nominally banned technology
laws.fullDescription: Satellite dishes for receiving foreign television broadcasts are illegal in Iran under a 1994 law. However, an estimated 70-80% of urban Iranians have satellite dishes, making enforcement essentially impossible. The government periodically conducts confiscation drives, particularly in the run-up to political events or after controversial broadcasts. The Persian-language satellite channels (BBC Persian, VOA Persian, Iran International, Manoto) broadcast news and entertainment to Iranian audiences. The selective enforcement creates a system of controlled tolerance.
laws.penalty: Fines and confiscation of equipment for illegal satellite dish possession
exceptions: Diplomatic residences and some hotels may legally receive satellite signals
Government buildings use approved satellite systems for official purposes
laws.source: Iranian Law on the Prevention of Use of Satellite Equipment, 1994

quiz.q: What percentage of urban Iranians are estimated to have illegal satellite dishes?
quiz.explanation: Despite the 1994 law banning satellite dishes, an estimated 70-80% of urban Iranians have them, making full enforcement impossible and creating a system of selective, politically-motivated enforcement rather than consistent application of the law.

laws.title: Renewable Energy — Solar and Wind
laws.subtitle: Iran's renewable energy development
laws.fullDescription: Iran has significant solar and wind energy potential, particularly in the desert regions of central and eastern Iran. The government has set renewable energy targets to reduce dependence on oil and gas for domestic power generation. Several wind and solar farms have been built. International sanctions have limited access to financing and technology for renewable energy projects. Iran's domestic companies have developed some capabilities in solar panel manufacturing. The government subsidizes energy prices heavily, which reduces incentives for efficiency.
laws.penalty: License violations subject to fines
exceptions: Off-grid rural electrification projects have simplified processes
Research and demonstration projects may have expedited approval
laws.source: Iranian Renewable Energy Organization (SUNA); Energy Ministry

quiz.q: What factor limits Iran's ability to develop renewable energy despite significant potential?
options: International sanctions limiting access to financing and technology
quiz.explanation: Despite significant solar and wind potential, Iran's renewable energy development is hampered by international sanctions that limit access to foreign financing, technology, and equipment, while domestic energy subsidies reduce efficiency incentives.

laws.title: Political Parties — Highly Restricted
laws.subtitle: Nominal multiparty system with severe constraints
laws.fullDescription: Iran nominally permits political parties but their operation is heavily constrained. Parties must be approved by the Interior Ministry and must conform to the principles of the Islamic Republic and Velayat-e Faqih. The Reformist Green Movement parties were shut down after the 2009 stolen election protests. Ethnic and minority parties are illegal. In practice, Iran has loose political tendencies (conservatives, moderate conservatives, reformists) rather than genuine political parties with independent programs. Opposition parties are banned.
laws.penalty: Criminal charges for members of unapproved parties
exceptions: Approved factions within the revolutionary framework can operate
Professional associations and guilds serve some quasi-political functions
laws.source: Iranian Political Parties, Coalitions and Groups Act, 1981

quiz.q: What happened to Iran's reformist political movements after the 2009 election protests?
options: Green Movement parties were shut down
They reorganized as the Democratic Movement
quiz.explanation: Following the 2009 disputed election and the Green Movement protests, reformist political parties and movements were shut down, their leaders placed under house arrest (Mousavi and Karroubi remain under house arrest), and political space for reformists dramatically narrowed.

laws.title: Iran-Iraq War — Legal Legacy
laws.subtitle: 1980-1988 war's lasting legal and social impacts
laws.fullDescription: The Iran-Iraq War (1980-1988) left deep legal and social imprints on Iranian society. Veterans' affairs are managed by the Bonyad Shahid (Martyrs Foundation) which provides benefits to families of those killed. The Basij forces were established during the war. The use of child soldiers (under 16) in the war remains a taboo topic. Iran's chemical weapons exposure (from Iraqi attacks) created a large population of chemical weapons survivors with ongoing medical needs. The war is a founding myth of the Islamic Republic.
laws.penalty: N/A — historical legacy
exceptions: Veterans receive special protections and benefits
War martyrs' families have privileged status in education and employment
laws.source: Bonyad Shahid; Iranian Veterans Law

quiz.q: What organization provides benefits to families of those killed in the Iran-Iraq War?
quiz.explanation: The Bonyad Shahid (Martyrs Foundation) provides benefits to families of those killed in the Iran-Iraq War and other conflicts, and is one of Iran's major bonyads with significant economic assets and political influence.

laws.title: Waqf — Islamic Endowments
laws.subtitle: Religious endowments holding vast property
laws.fullDescription: Waqf (Islamic endowments) are perpetual charitable trusts where property is dedicated to religious or charitable purposes. The Endowments and Charitable Affairs Organization manages registered waqf in Iran. Major religious sites (including the Astan Quds Razavi managing the Imam Reza shrine in Mashhad) operate as waqf institutions controlling vast property and businesses. Waqf property cannot be bought or sold. The waqf system predates the Islamic Republic and represents another layer of religiously-controlled economic activity outside normal market rules.
laws.penalty: Criminal penalties for unauthorized use or sale of waqf property
exceptions: Emergency circumstances may allow temporary modification of waqf conditions
State can manage waqf property for public purposes in certain circumstances
laws.source: Iranian Endowments and Charitable Affairs Organization

quiz.q: What major shrine institution in Mashhad operates as a waqf and controls vast economic assets?
quiz.explanation: The Astan Quds Razavi, which manages the Imam Reza shrine in Mashhad, is one of the world's wealthiest waqf institutions, controlling vast real estate, businesses, and cultural assets, and is closely linked to the Supreme Leader's office.

laws.title: Iran and International Law
laws.subtitle: Iran's selective engagement with international law
laws.fullDescription: Iran has ratified many international human rights treaties (ICCPR, ICESCR, CRC, CAT) while systematically violating them. Iran argues that international human rights law must be interpreted through Islamic law, a position that allows it to reject obligations that conflict with its religious legal system. Iran does not accept the compulsory jurisdiction of the International Court of Justice for human rights matters. The UN Human Rights Council has a Special Rapporteur on Iran. Iran rejects most UN criticism as interference in internal affairs.
laws.penalty: N/A — international law compliance issue
exceptions: Iran cooperates with some UN technical assistance programs
Regional MENA human rights mechanisms are limited in scope
laws.source: UN Human Rights Treaty Bodies; Iranian Treaty Ratifications

quiz.q: On what basis does Iran argue it can reject international human rights obligations?
options: As a developing country with different priorities
That international treaties were signed under duress
That international human rights law must be interpreted through Islamic law
That only regional (OIC) human rights standards apply
quiz.explanation: Iran argues that international human rights norms must be interpreted through Islamic law, providing a basis to reject specific obligations that conflict with its Islamic legal system, particularly regarding gender equality, religious freedom, and criminal punishments.

laws.title: Mining Sector — Labor Conditions
laws.subtitle: Mine worker safety and labor rights
laws.fullDescription: Iran has significant mining resources including iron ore, copper, zinc, and other minerals. Mine accidents are frequent due to safety standard failures. The Tabas coal mine disaster (2019) killed 43 miners due to methane gas explosion. Mining workers' wages are often delayed or unpaid, leading to protests. The Ministry of Industries, Mining and Trade oversees the sector. Workers' safety councils required by law are often inactive in practice. Iran's mining sector is a site of significant labor activism.
laws.penalty: Employer liability for mine accidents; criminal negligence charges in serious cases
exceptions: State-owned mines may have different enforcement standards
IRGC-linked mining companies operate with reduced oversight
laws.source: Iranian Mining Law; Labour Law applications to mining sector

quiz.q: What caused the 2019 Tabas coal mine disaster in Iran?
quiz.explanation: The 2019 Tabas coal mine disaster killed 43 miners due to a methane gas explosion, one of Iran's worst recent mine disasters and reflecting ongoing safety standard failures in Iran's mining sector.

laws.title: Juvenile Justice
laws.subtitle: Age of criminal responsibility under Islamic law
laws.fullDescription: Iran's Islamic Penal Code (2013) sets the age of criminal responsibility at puberty — 15 lunar years for boys and 9 lunar years for girls. This means girls as young as 8.5 solar years can be held criminally responsible. The 2013 reforms introduced provisions for courts to order psychological evaluation for juvenile offenders facing death penalty, potentially commuting to reformatory detention. However, Iran continues to execute juvenile offenders and has one of the world's highest rates of executing persons for crimes committed as minors.
laws.penalty: Death penalty applicable in principle for serious offenses from age of puberty
exceptions: 2013 reforms allow psychological evaluation that may substitute for death penalty
International pressure has commuted some juvenile death sentences
laws.source: Iranian Islamic Penal Code, 2013, Articles 90-92

quiz.q: What age of criminal responsibility does Iranian law set for girls under Islamic jurisprudence?
quiz.explanation: Under Iran's Islamic Penal Code, girls reach the age of criminal responsibility at 9 lunar years (approximately 8.5 solar years) — the Islamic legal definition of puberty for girls — one of the lowest ages of criminal responsibility globally.

laws.title: Industrial Pollution — Petrochemical Industry
laws.subtitle: Environmental damage from petrochemical sector
laws.fullDescription: Iran has a large petrochemical industry, particularly in Khuzestan and Assaluyeh on the Persian Gulf. Industrial pollution from petrochemical plants, steel mills, and cement factories causes significant air, water, and soil pollution. Local communities in industrial areas face serious health impacts. Environmental impact assessments are required but not always enforced. Workers in Khuzestan's oil industry have protested both labor conditions and pollution impacts on local communities and water sources.
laws.penalty: EPA fines for industrial pollution; criminal penalties for serious environmental crimes
exceptions: Strategic industries may receive regulatory relief
Emergency repairs to prevent larger pollution events prioritized
laws.source: Iranian Environmental Protection Organization; Khuzestan industrial case studies

quiz.q: Which Iranian province contains the largest concentration of petrochemical and oil industry facilities?
quiz.explanation: Khuzestan Province in southwestern Iran contains the largest concentration of Iran's petrochemical facilities, oil refineries, and steel mills, and its communities face significant industrial pollution affecting air, water, and soil quality.

laws.title: Nowruz — Persian New Year Legal Status
laws.subtitle: Persian cultural celebrations preserved in Islamic Republic
laws.fullDescription: Nowruz (Persian New Year, celebrated on the spring equinox) is observed as a national holiday in Iran despite initial tensions with the Islamic Republic, which viewed some pre-Islamic Persian traditions with suspicion. Ayatollah Khomeini initially criticized Nowruz celebrations but the holiday was preserved given its deep cultural significance. Nowruz traditions include house cleaning, visiting family, and setting the Haft-Sin table. The holiday is also celebrated by Azerbaijani, Kurdish, and other communities in Iran and the broader region.
laws.penalty: N/A — national holiday
exceptions: Some stricter Islamic groups observe Nowruz with reduced celebration
International Nowruz Day recognized by UN General Assembly
laws.source: Iranian National Holidays Law; UNESCO Nowruz Intangible Cultural Heritage

quiz.q: When does Iran celebrate Nowruz (Persian New Year)?
options: First day of the Islamic New Year
The birthday of the Prophet Muhammad
quiz.explanation: Nowruz is celebrated on the spring equinox (around March 20-21) and marks the Persian New Year according to the Solar Hijri calendar used in Iran. It is one of humanity's oldest celebrations and was recognized as UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage.

laws.title: Intelligence Apparatus — MOIS and IRGC Intel
laws.subtitle: Parallel intelligence services
laws.fullDescription: Iran has two primary intelligence services: the Ministry of Intelligence (MOIS/VEVAK) and the IRGC Intelligence Organization. The two services sometimes compete and have conflicting jurisdictions. Both have been implicated in human rights violations, assassinations of dissidents abroad, and domestic political suppression. The 1998 'Chain Murders' of dissidents were attributed to MOIS rogue elements. The IRGC Intelligence controls Ward 209 of Evin Prison. Iran's intelligence services have conducted operations in Europe, North America, and throughout the Middle East.
laws.penalty: Citizens targeted by intelligence services have no effective legal recourse
exceptions: Intelligence operations classified and outside judicial oversight
Diplomatic immunity protects some intelligence officers abroad
laws.source: MOIS Establishment Law; IRGC Intelligence Organization

quiz.q: What 1998 events were attributed to rogue elements of Iran's Ministry of Intelligence (MOIS)?
options: The 'Chain Murders' of Iranian dissident intellectuals
quiz.explanation: The 1998 'Chain Murders' — a series of killings of Iranian dissident writers, intellectuals, and political activists — were attributed to rogue elements within the Ministry of Intelligence (MOIS) and led to a major political crisis under President Khatami.

laws.title: Religious Education — Mandatory Islamic Studies
laws.subtitle: Compulsory Islamic curriculum in all schools
laws.fullDescription: Islamic religious education is mandatory at all levels of Iranian schooling. The curriculum includes Quran recitation, Islamic theology, and religious ethics. Non-Muslim students (from recognized minorities) may be partially exempted from Islamic content. The education system emphasizes the values of the Islamic Republic and loyalty to the Supreme Leader. Textbooks are centrally produced and contain politically approved content. Critical thinking about religion or politics is not encouraged in the curriculum.
laws.penalty: N/A — mandatory educational curriculum
exceptions: Recognized minority students may have some religious exemptions
Private international schools have limited curriculum modifications
laws.source: Iranian Ministry of Education Curriculum Framework

quiz.q: Is Islamic religious education mandatory in Iran's school system?
options: Mandatory at all levels of the state school system
quiz.explanation: Islamic religious education is mandatory at all levels of Iran's state school system, including Quran recitation, Islamic theology, and religious ethics, with the curriculum centrally produced to reflect the values of the Islamic Republic.

laws.title: Journalist Arrests — Press Freedom
laws.subtitle: Iran among world's leading jailers of journalists
laws.fullDescription: Iran consistently ranks among the world's top jailers of journalists, alongside China. The Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ) and Reporters Without Borders document dozens of Iranian journalists imprisoned at any given time. Charges used against journalists include 'propaganda against the state,' 'insulting the Supreme Leader,' espionage, and national security offenses. Foreign journalists require government accreditation that can be revoked. Iranian journalists working for foreign media face particularly severe risks.
laws.penalty: Imprisonment 1-15 years under various national security charges
exceptions: State media journalists operate freely within approved parameters
Selected international media may receive occasional accreditation for specific events
laws.source: Committee to Protect Journalists; Reporters Without Borders Iran Index

quiz.q: Which organizations document Iran's journalist imprisonments?
options: Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ) and Reporters Without Borders
quiz.explanation: Both the Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ) and Reporters Without Borders (RSF) consistently document Iran as one of the world's leading jailers of journalists, with dozens imprisoned at any given time on national security and press law charges.

laws.title: Iran's Geopolitical Position
laws.subtitle: Constitutional foreign policy in regional context
laws.fullDescription: Iran's constitution and foreign policy position Iran as a revolutionary Islamic state in opposition to Western 'imperialism' and Israeli 'Zionism.' Article 3(16) of the constitution calls for non-alignment and non-interference, while Articles 152-154 support liberation movements. Iran's 'Axis of Resistance' (Hezbollah, Hamas, Houthis, Iraqi militias) represents the operational expression of this constitutional policy. Iran's geopolitical position affects all aspects of its domestic law, particularly through sanctions and security legislation.
laws.penalty: N/A — foreign policy framework affecting domestic security law
exceptions: Pragmatic economic relationships coexist with official hostility to the West
China and Russia maintain extensive ties with Iran despite tensions
laws.source: Iranian Constitution, Articles 3, 152-154

quiz.q: What does Iran call its network of allied forces in the Middle East?
quiz.explanation: Iran calls its network of allied proxy forces — including Hezbollah in Lebanon, Hamas in Gaza, the Houthis in Yemen, and various Iraqi militias — the 'Axis of Resistance,' framing it as resistance to Western imperialism and Israeli policy.

laws.title: Iranian Diaspora — Legal Status
laws.subtitle: Millions of Iranians abroad and their relationship to Iranian law
laws.fullDescription: An estimated 4-5 million Iranians live abroad, with large communities in the US, Germany, UK, Canada, UAE, and Sweden. Iran does not recognize renunciation of Iranian citizenship, meaning most Iranians abroad remain Iranian citizens under Iranian law regardless of other nationalities acquired. This means Iranian-born persons traveling to Iran can be arrested and treated as Iranian nationals. The diaspora is politically divided between supporters and opponents of the Islamic Republic. Diaspora media (BBC Persian, Iran International) is highly influential.
laws.penalty: Dual nationals arrested in Iran face prosecution as Iranian citizens with no consular access from their other country
exceptions: Those who left before 1979 may have different status in practice
Naturalized citizens of some countries may have reduced risk in practice
laws.source: Iranian Nationality Law; Expatriate Affairs Organization

quiz.q: How many Iranians are estimated to live abroad?
quiz.explanation: An estimated 4-5 million Iranians live abroad, with major diaspora communities in the United States, Germany, United Kingdom, Canada, and UAE. Iran does not recognize renunciation of citizenship, maintaining legal jurisdiction over diaspora members who return.

laws.title: Iran's Future — Reform vs. Revolution
laws.subtitle: Debate between internal reform and fundamental change
laws.fullDescription: Iran's political future involves a fundamental debate between those who believe in gradual reform within the Islamic Republic's framework and those who seek fundamental systemic change. The 2022 Woman, Life, Freedom protests represented the most serious challenge to the Islamic Republic since 1979, with protesters explicitly calling for an end to the theocratic system rather than reform. The aging Supreme Leader's succession will be a critical moment. International nuclear and human rights pressures continue. Iran's young, educated population increasingly demands change.
laws.penalty: N/A — political and constitutional context
exceptions: Constitutional reform possible in theory through Supreme Leader approval
Mass social pressure has historically led to some tactical concessions
laws.source: Iranian Constitutional Framework; Political Reform Debates

quiz.q: What distinguished the 2022 Woman, Life, Freedom protests from earlier reform movements in Iran?
options: They were smaller than previous protests
They only demanded better economic conditions
Protesters explicitly called for ending the theocratic system, not just reform within it
They were led by political parties rather than spontaneous protesters
quiz.explanation: The 2022 Woman, Life, Freedom protests were distinguished from earlier reform movements (like the 2009 Green Movement) by explicitly calling for an end to the theocratic Islamic Republic system itself, not just reform within it — representing a generational shift in Iranian political demands.
